Section 1. 공소기각 결정을 overlooking 한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that even based on the facts stated in the indictment, there is no specific statement of the constitutional-subversion purpose, riotous acts, and conspiracy content, which are elements of insurrection, or of the division of execution in the co-principal murder charge, so because the facts charged are not sufficiently specified, an order dismissing the prosecution should have been entered under Article 373(1)4 of the Military Court-Martial Act, but the lower court overlooked this and thereby misunderstood the above legal principles. 먼저 this point를 consider한다.

Upon review, this issue was already lawfully considered by the lower court. In addition, the facts charged against the Defendants, as organized from the indictment and the two applications to amend the indictment, are sufficiently specified on their face and are also admitted to be specifically stated. Further, regarding Defendant C’s murder charge, the indictment clearly accuses co-principal liability by conspiracy, so the omission of facts concerning execution division cannot be deemed a defect. Therefore, this argument is without merit.

Section 2. Procedural illegality

1. 불고불리 원칙 위반

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that according to the indictment and the amendment application, Defendant G was prosecuted for killing T and U with the purpose of subverting the Constitution, but the lower judgment found him to have killed six persons, namely B, T, V, W, X, and U, which is plainly a violation of the principle of accusation and adjudication and thus unlawful. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the amendment application lawfully granted at the first trial date in the lower court, it is clear that Defendant G was prosecuted for having killed T and U, among the six deceased persons in this case, for the purpose of subverting the Constitution. However, in the reasoning portion of the lower judgment, the court stated in the conclusion on murder with insurrectionary purpose that “from around 19:40 to 20:05 on the same day, former President B, the said T, the said V, the said W, the said X, and the said U were each caused to die, thereby the Defendants jointly murdered the above victims for the purpose of subverting the Constitution.” On its face this seems to have committed the alleged illegality. Nevertheless, the lower court had earlier stated that on October 26, 1979 around 19:40, Defendant G, after the other Defendants had fired at the deceased persons, received around 20:05 that day an instruction from Defendant E to carry out a confirmation shot on persons not yet fully dead and agreed to participate in that killing. Not only that, but the lower court also stated that the shooting pursuant to that instruction consisted of firing “one shot at the said W lying fallen, two shots at the said V, two shots at the said T groaning, and one shot at the said U lying fallen and groaning.” In view of this, although the expression in the conclusion is somewhat inaccurate, the lower court is still recognized as having judged within the scope of the prosecution. This argument has no merit.

2. 「공개재판」 위반

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the first-instance military court on the second trial date of December 8, 1979, conducted the defense counsel’s cross-examination of Defendant A in closed session without satisfying the prescribed requirements, and also on the ninth trial date of December 18, 1979, effectively barred public access and proceeded with Defendant A’s final statement without even entering a closure decision, so the closed proceedings were clearly illegal in their grounds and procedure. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the record, on the second trial date of December 8, 1979, during defense counsel’s cross-examination of Defendant A, the court ordered a closed proceeding because Defendant A, as former Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, had performed important duties concerning foreign intelligence, domestic security intelligence, security work relating to state secrets, insurrection, foreign relations, investigation of crimes prescribed in the National Security Act and Anti-Communist Act, and coordination and supervision of intelligence and security affairs, and because the defendant’s statements in court in response to that cross-examination substantially included matters that might interfere with the security or public order of the State. The proceedings thereafter were closed. This was based on Article 67 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which provides that “the oral proceedings and judgment in trial shall be public; provided, however, that where public order may be disturbed, morals harmed, or where necessary for military secrecy, the military court may decide not to hold them publicly.” Even in light of the record, the reason is fully understandable. Thus the first-instance measure was proper and cannot be said to have been mistaken. Accordingly, this part of the argument is without merit.

Further, whether a stage of the trial proceedings was public must be entered in the trial transcript under Article 85(2)5 of the Military Court-Martial Act, and Article 89 provides that matters recorded in the transcript as procedural acts on a trial date are proved by that transcript alone. Therefore, whether the proceedings on December 18, 1979, the ninth trial date in the first instance, were public can be established only by the transcript in this case. The first-instance ninth trial transcript states in the column for public/private that the trial was “public in court.” Hence the proceedings on that date can be recognized as having been conducted in a public courtroom. Accordingly, this argument also lacks merit.

3. 신문제한의 illegality

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the first instance and the lower court, although under Article 344 of the Military Court-Martial Act they could limit examination only to the extent that the essential rights of the parties were not harmed, nevertheless restricted examination and statements whenever specific references were to be made in the course of examining Defendant A concerning the motive and purpose of the act, the domestic political situation immediately before the act, and the inevitability of the act, and also frequently imposed limitations during the examination of Defendants E and F, thereby gravely infringing the Defendants’ and counsel’s defense rights beyond permissible bounds. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the first-instance and appellate transcripts, it can be recognized that the court afforded the above Defendants necessary and sufficient opportunities to make statements, and each defense counsel was granted the necessary right to examine the Defendants and other parties; further, each defense counsel had necessary and sufficient opportunities to defend the Defendants, and each Defendant had a full opportunity to make final statements. Particularly in Defendant A’s case, from the content of the statements in response to examinations by the prosecutor, defense counsel, and legal officer in the first-instance and appellate courts, as well as the supplemental statement of appeal grounds submitted by Defendant A himself and the statements of grounds of appeal submitted by his counsel, it is recognized that the defense content alleged by the appellant is sufficiently reflected. Therefore, the contrary argument lacks merit.

4. 퇴정명령의 illegality

Among the Grounds of Appeal, when questioning Defendant C and others at the third trial date on December 10, 1979, the first-instance court, invoking Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, ordered Defendant A to withdraw from the courtroom on the ground that he could not make sufficient statements in Defendant A’s presence; this, it is argued, was done without just cause solely on the prosecutor’s motion, and further, after Defendant C’s statement ended, Defendant A, who had been withdrawn, should have been brought back in and informed of the substance, and allowed to question Defendant C directly, but instead the proceedings were simply closed without bringing Defendant A back that day. This is said to be illegal. We consider this argument.

Upon review, according to the first-instance third trial transcript, before the examination of Defendant C at that third trial date, the first-instance court, ex officio, ordered the remaining Defendants including Defendant A to withdraw on the ground that they were deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of co-defendants. This measure was based on Article 343(2) of the Military Court-Martial Act, which allows the presiding judge to order withdrawal when, on his own motion or upon application by the prosecutor, the defendant is deemed unable to make sufficient statements in the presence of another defendant. In light of the record, this was reasonable. It is true that after Defendant C’s statement ended, the proceedings were closed without Defendant A being brought back. However, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, when the court resumed and at the fourth trial date the legal officer informed all defendants and counsel present of the substance of the prior hearing regarding Defendant C and asked their views, the parties said they had no particular opinion; this is clearly shown in the record. Further, according to the first-instance sixth trial transcript, Defendant A’s assigned counsel O and Y cross-examined Defendant C on Defendant A’s behalf. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

5. 증인신문절차의 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, first, according to the witness examination record of Z adopted by the lower court, it is clear that Defendant A was not allowed to participate in the examination of that witness. This, it is argued, violated the law guaranteeing a defendant’s right to participate in witness examination and thereby the right of cross-examination. Second, it is argued that in examining witnesses, there was no service of summons by the prescribed procedure under Articles 106 through 108 of the Military Court-Martial Act; moreover, in some cases witnesses were made to wait before the prosecutor had even applied for evidence, and then were taken up and examined immediately upon application, which was not only a procedural violation but a grave illegality depriving the Defendants and their counsel of the opportunity to prepare for cross-examination. We consider this argument.

Upon review, first, according to the first-instance trial record, at the eighth trial date attended by all Defendants and counsel, concerning witness Z who failed to appear, the first-instance court instructed the legal officer that the witness would be examined outside the courtroom and ordered the relevant persons to attend, and thereafter on December 17, 1979, legal officer AA examined the witness at the Army Headquarters Judge Advocate General’s Office, where Defendant C and his counsel and the counsel for Defendants A and D were present. In the manner of that witness examination, it cannot be said that Defendant A was not notified and thus denied participation. Moreover, the witness’s testimony primarily concerned Defendant C’s criminal facts, so no illegality in procedure can be found. In addition, according to the same trial record, at the ninth trial date resumed on December 18, 1979, the first-instance court, after the legal officer informed the courtroom that witness Z had been examined, presented the substance and asked for the parties’ opinions; the parties stated that they had no particular opinion. Therefore, even if there were a mistake as alleged, since the Defendants and counsel stated at the evidence examination that they had no particular opinion, the mistake would be cured by waiver of the right to object. Accordingly, this part of the argument is without merit.

Second, according to the first-instance trial record, after the first-instance court selected eight witnesses at the sixth trial date, it examined the two selected witnesses who appeared at the seventh trial date, and at the eighth trial date it newly selected nine witnesses present at the court and examined those witnesses and the five previously selected witnesses who appeared. Also, one witness examination was conducted outside the courtroom by legal officer AA on December 17, 1979. Under the proviso of Article 192 of the Military Court-Martial Act, witnesses present in court may be examined without summons, so it cannot be illegal that the nine present witnesses were not summoned. Nor can it necessarily be faulted that those witnesses were examined immediately upon application. As to the remaining witnesses, although summons procedures should have been taken, no trace of issuance of summons can be found in the record except that the transcripts state they were summoned and appeared. However, after examining those witnesses and the witness outside the courtroom, the first-instance court afforded the Defendants and their counsel the opportunity to state their opinions in court or at the next trial date, and they stated that they had no particular opinion. Moreover, it is clearly shown in the record that the Defendants and counsel conducted sufficient and necessary cross-examination of those witnesses. Therefore, the defect of non-issuance of summons cannot be said to affect the judgment outcome, and this portion of the argument also cannot be accepted.

6. 변호인 없이 개정한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, in military court cases counsel is mandatory under Articles 62 and 315 of the Military Court-Martial Act, and therefore proceedings cannot be opened without counsel’s appearance. Nevertheless, on January 22, 1980, at the first trial date, as a measure under Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act rather than severance of trial, the lower court opened proceedings with only Defendants C and G present and without the appearance of Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel, and is alleged to have unlawfully examined matters concerning the motives and circumstances of the co-defendants’ offenses. We consider this argument.

Upon review of the appellate trial record, after notifying Defendants A, E, and F and their counsel that the first trial date was set for January 22, 1980, the court later re-designated and notified the trial date as January 23, 1980. Then, at the first trial date on January 22, 1980, the court, pursuant to Article 416 of the Military Court-Martial Act, deemed that some Defendants including A, E, and F need not appear at trial and did not order their appearance, but proceeded with the hearing with only Defendants C and G present. Article 416 is only the provision that in appellate proceedings the appeal instance is not a de novo trial but a post hoc review of specific factual and legal issues in the first-instance judgment, and thus as a rule the defendant need not appear at appellate trial dates. It is not a provision allowing only some co-defendants to appear selectively and excusing the others. Therefore, the above measure of the appellate court was mistaken. However, at the continued second trial date on January 23, 1980, the legal officer informed the substance of the important matters from the previous hearing, and thereafter sufficient opportunity for cross-examination was afforded. Moreover, the record shows that the first instance had already conducted sufficient hearings on the matters alleged in the appeal grounds, and at the first appellate trial date there is no indication that new matters were examined on that point. Accordingly, the error was not such as to affect the outcome of the judgment. The Supreme Court decisions cited by the appellant are not apt to this case. Thus, this argument also cannot be accepted.

7. 변호권의 박탈

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the Defendants’ lineal family members and spouse have, under Article 59 of the Military Court-Martial Act, an independent right to appoint counsel. Thus, even if the defendant himself refuses to argue, the right of counsel appointed by the lineal family members and spouse does not extinguish. Nevertheless, counsel AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s lineal family members and spouse were denied entry into the courtroom by military police serving as courtroom order personnel pursuant to the judge’s order at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, and it is argued that thereby their right to counsel was deprived, and that the court committed illegality in failing to decide on the objection to this point. We consider this argument.

Upon review, even if the defendant’s lineal family members and spouse may independently appoint counsel under Article 59(2), the appointing party independently exercises the principal’s appointing right, so the effect of the appointment extends to the principal, and the principal must be understood as being able to revoke the appointment. In this case, according to the first-instance fourth trial transcript, while the hearing proceeded with privately retained counsel including attorneys AB and others appointed by Defendant A’s mother and spouse, Defendant A stated, “From now on, I refuse the defense by the private defense team for this defendant.” At that time the legal officer informed him that the military court requires counsel and that, if privately retained counsel must be dismissed, assigned counsel must be appointed. Defendant A then stated, “Please appoint assigned counsel for this defendant; I will revoke all privately retained counsel for myself.” This is clearly shown in the record. Therefore, the above private counsel were lawfully revoked, and the fact that they were later denied entry to the courtroom as counsel at the first-instance fifth trial date on December 12, 1979, cannot be regarded as deprivation of the right to counsel. Nor can it be said that any illegality occurred merely because the objection was not decided. This argument is without merit.

8. 공판조서 미비와 열람등 사권의 박탈

Among the Grounds of Appeal, even if the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act requiring trial transcripts to be promptly prepared within five days after each trial date, considering Articles 89, 86, and 64 of the Military Court-Martial Act, etc., the transcript in military court proceedings should also be prepared before the next trial date or at the latest before the factual hearing ends. Nevertheless, it is argued that the first instance and the appellate court did not promptly prepare the transcripts, thereby effectively depriving counsel of the right under Article 64 to inspect and copy the transcripts. We consider this argument.

Upon review, the Military Court-Martial Act does not contain a provision like Article 54 of the Criminal Procedure Act setting a statutory period for preparing transcripts. Of course, military court transcripts must also be prepared promptly, but one cannot definitively say by when they must be completed. In particular, even the statutory period set by the Criminal Procedure Act is only a directive provision, and merely failing to complete the transcript within that period cannot by itself render the transcript void. Therefore, no fault can be found with respect to the timing of preparation of the first-instance and appellate transcripts; nor can it be said that there was illegality in depriving the right of inspection and copying. The gist of the argument is that it concerns the defendants’ defense rights. Reviewing the first-instance and appellate records, it is recognized that the defendants’ defense rights were fully protected; accordingly, this argument cannot be accepted.

9. 재판의 독립성 침해

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the first instance and the appellate court pressed ahead with the hearing as if there were a fixed predetermined schedule under the aforementioned unlawful procedures infringing the defendants’ defense rights and right to counsel, and that even during the hearing, notes of contact from outside were publicly and repeatedly handed to the judges through the back door behind the judges’ bench; this, it is argued, violated Article 102 of the Constitution and Article 28 of the Military Court-Martial Act, which guarantee judicial independence. We consider this argument.

As to the arguments alleging that the above first-instance and appellate procedures were illegal, we have already found them to be without merit. Even in light of the record, it is not recognized that the factual hearings in the first instance and appellate court were pressed ahead under some fixed schedule as alleged. Rather, the record only shows that the first instance conducted sufficient factual hearings eight times across the second through ninth trial dates, and the appellate court did so three times across the first through third trial dates, while ensuring the defendants’ defense rights and right to counsel. No other illegality is found. Furthermore, there is absolutely nothing in the record suggesting that contact notes were delivered to the judges during the hearing, and especially whether their content infringed judicial independence is wholly unknown. This point is too abstract and fabricated to require further discussion. Therefore, the argument lacks merit.

Section 3. 검찰관 작성의 피의자신문조서에 대한 「voluntariness」 issue

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that the suspect-interrogation records concerning the Defendants prepared by the prosecutor were merely an extension of the records prepared by the military police investigators because, at the time of the prosecutor’s interrogation, the Defendants were physically and mentally exhausted by numerous acts of torture at the joint investigation headquarters under martial law, and in particular Defendant A made statements involuntarily under the prosecutor’s earnest persuasion while his consciousness was dim due to aggravation of his chronic liver disease; or because the prosecutor conducted the interrogation at the place where the military judicial police had investigated after receiving the case, under a state in which access and communication with counsel and family were completely prohibited, and the record content was the same as the military judicial police records except for legal refinement, so it lacked voluntariness. It is argued that the lower court nevertheless used this as evidence of guilt, thereby committing an error of law concerning evidentiary capacity or a defect for failure to provide reasons, and also erred by omitting consideration of the Grounds of Appeal. We consider this argument. (This point relates to the argument below that the fact-finding violated the rules of evidence, and for convenience it is considered separately.)

Upon review, in general, absence of voluntariness in a statement means that the person being interrogated by an investigative authority did not make the statement under free conditions because of threats, torture, or other means. Determination of voluntariness is made within a reasonable scope by the free conviction of the judge without violating the rules of experience. It suffices that the adjudicating panel makes a reasonable judgment in all respects of the litigation process, namely the preparation and content of the document, the defendant’s explanation and demeanor, the prosecutor’s elucidations, and the testimony of witnesses involved in the preparation of the document. On that basis, the record shows the following:

(1) At the second trial date in the first instance, during the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A:
Q: “When the prosecutor investigated, I wrote the record and made you verify it item by item, did I not?”
A: “Yes.”
Q: “After confirming the contents, you signed and affixed your seal, did you not?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 210)

(2) At the third trial date in the first instance, during the prosecutor’s direct examination of Defendant A:
Q: “During the prosecutor’s investigation, was there any instance in which you made a statement under compulsion or threat?”
A: “I said, please write it as it was.”
(Trial transcript p. 247)
and:
Q: “When the prosecutor investigated, was there any threat or coercion?”
A: “No.”
Q: “You reviewed the record prepared at that time, confirmed the contents, and signed and affixed your seal, did you not?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 256)

(3) During the cross-examination of Defendant A by defense counsel AC at the first appellate trial date:
Q: “Looking at the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation record concerning the defendant, it says that during a conversation at the curb in front of the entrance you nodded your head and thought you would kill T, and where was that record prepared?”
A: “I do not know the exact location, but the prosecutor came to the Joint Investigation Headquarters and took the record for two days.”
Q: “Was there no investigation at the Prosecutor’s Office?”
A: “There was. After that, they came to the Judge Advocate General’s Office twice and investigated me.”
Q: “Then, did the prosecutor investigate you on the spot immediately after the Joint Investigation Headquarters investigation?”
A: “No. After the case was transferred to the Prosecutor’s Office, the prosecutor came to that place and investigated me.”
Q: “At that time, did you clearly know that the case had been transferred to the prosecutor?”
A: “I clearly knew that the case had been transferred to the prosecutor and that he was a military prosecutor.”
(Trial transcript pp. 1398-1400)

(4) During the cross-examination of Defendant F by his counsel Y at the fifth trial date in the first instance:
Q: “When you were investigated before the prosecutor, did you tell the truth and read the contents?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 430)

(5) During the cross-examination of Defendant G by his counsel P at the same trial date:
Q: “Did the prosecutor write the record as you said?”
A: “Yes.”
(Trial transcript p. 435)

(6) Through the hearings in the first instance and appellate court, there is no statement to be found that the Defendants were investigated under a non-free atmosphere such as assault or deception during the prosecutor’s interrogation of suspects.

(7) According to the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records, the Defendants’ statements are almost identical in content concerning the circumstances and details of the offense in this case, with only some differences in expression, and in particular as for Defendants C, D, E, and G, they were investigated on two occasions and the statements on both occasions are consistent.

(8) In the first-instance and appellate hearings as well, the Defendants’ statements in court are largely the same as the contents of the prosecutor’s statements regarding objective facts, differing only as to some subjective matters such as motive, and this becomes even more pronounced as the proceedings progress. These facts are apparent from the record. Taking these together with other circumstances appearing in the record, the prosecutor-prepared suspect-interrogation records for the Defendants are all admitted to have voluntariness. Therefore, the lower court’s use of them as evidence of guilt was proper, and there is no illegality as alleged. Accordingly, this part of the argument lacks merit.

And although Defendant C’s counsel AC raised this point in the statement of grounds of appeal submitted, the lower court’s failure to decide it was mistaken; however, since the argument is plainly without merit as above, the mistake could not have affected the outcome of the judgment. Therefore, this point also lacks merit.

Section 4. 범죄구성요건에 관한 위법

1. 「국헌문란」의 목적

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the “subversion of the Constitution” prescribed in Article 91 of the Criminal Act, as the purpose element of the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, ultimately means everything that unlawfully destroys the State’s political basic order itself. The political basic order of our country is, needless to say, a liberal democratic political system; therefore only acts that substantially or formally destroy the principle of popular sovereignty and the people’s fundamental freedoms and equality would constitute subversion of the Constitution. Accordingly, overthrow of a specific government or cabinet, or shouting slogans of overthrow, or whether the means of overthrowing is violence, or killing a specific constitutional organ as a natural person and planning succession or improvement thereof, would not fall under this.

First, in the case of Defendant A, the Yushin system, by its establishment and continuance alone, was not only an illegal criminal state in which sovereignty was usurped, but its content and operation produced a continuing condition that destroyed the political basic order of a democratic state. Therefore, for Defendant A, the killing of the President, a natural person, was unavoidably done according to a plan long prepared for the restoration of democracy. Even if not so, since after this offense he intended to enact a democratic constitution and organize the National Assembly and Government by democratic methods, there was no purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Second, in the case of Defendant C, it is difficult to conclude, merely because he killed T, the head of the Presidential Security Service, who was not even a state organ established by the Constitution, that he had a purpose of subverting the Constitution like the co-defendants; and as to Defendant C, neither his own statement nor his external behavior can be said to show a purpose of subverting the Constitution.

Third, in the case of Defendant D, he merely thought that only a few persons would be killed and the President abducted in this offense, and the killing of security officer V and the like, which he admits was done pursuant to the order of his superior, would not amount to subversion of the Constitution. Moreover, Defendant A’s explanation also states that he reached this offense in order to restore liberal democracy, so it cannot be said that there was a purpose to subvert the Constitution.

Fourth, in the case of Defendants E, F, and G, the Defendants were merely security guards or drivers of the Central Intelligence Agency restaurant and, having no choice, blindly and mechanically carried out the orders of Defendant D, the chief responsible person there. They could not even imagine the specific harm and consequences. In particular, Defendant G did not know of the murder of the President or even of its plan. Nevertheless, the lower court found, contrary to Defendant C’s explanation, that the facts it held satisfied the purpose of subverting the Constitution, and as to the other Defendants, it found that they had carried out riots or killings with the purpose of subverting the Constitution on the ground that they knew a state of national upheaval had occurred. It is argued that this was a fact-finding without evidence including corroboration required by strict proof, a violation of the rules of evidence contrary to logic and experience, a failure of hearing especially concerning the specific method after the act, and a defect for lack of reasons because there were no factual statements that could constitute a purpose to subvert the Constitution; or that the legal principles concerning the purpose of subversion of the Constitution in the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection were misunderstood. We consider this argument.

(1) First, we examine the legal principles concerning the purpose of subversion of the Constitution.

Article 91 of the Criminal Act provides that in this Chapter, “purpose of subverting the Constitution” means the following, and defines it: 1. abolishing the functions of the Constitution or laws without following the procedures prescribed by the Constitution or laws; 2. overthrowing, by force, a state organ established by the Constitution or making the exercise of its functions impossible. This ultimately means unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws. As argued, it does not necessarily have an extra-legal meaning, and certainly does not mean changing to a communist, monarchical, or dictatorial system. Of course, as argued, killing only a natural person who is a specific state organ, or planning his succession, does not fall under it. Further, since the crime of insurrection is a crime with a specific purpose, the general principles concerning crimes with specific purpose apply. The purpose belongs to matters requiring strict proof and must be direct, but it cannot be said that it requires a desire or will for the result to occur, nor does it require definite knowledge; conditional awareness is sufficient.

(2) Next, we examine the lower court’s factual findings on this point regarding the Defendants.

(A) Part concerning Defendant A

The lower judgment stated the following as the facts of Defendant A’s purpose of subverting the Constitution: Defendant A, while performing his duties as Director of the Central Intelligence Agency, saw his plans for stabilizing the political situation repeatedly fail, exposing his incompetence, and after being reprimanded by former President B, rumors of dismissal circulated, causing him to feel insecure in his position. Meanwhile, although he resented the President’s greater trust in T, then head of the Presidential Security Service, who was junior to him and younger, despite T’s arrogant attitude and interference beyond his authority, he planned to seize power after killing the President, and for secrecy independently devised the concrete plan for the act. After assassinating the President, he planned to declare martial law on the ground of national security and public disorder, to use the authority and organizational force of the Central Intelligence Agency to take control of the martial law forces and suppress the situation by force, to constitute a revolutionary committee overseeing legislative, judicial, and executive powers, to assume the chairmanship himself and secure a basis of power, and then to run for President. Examining the important basis of this conclusion from the evidence lawfully admitted and cited by the lower court:

(a) Defendant A’s statements

1) “Q: Why did you call the Army Chief of Staff and ... to the vicinity of the accident site?
A: I lured them from the outset for use after the act; after the act, I would come immediately, keep the Army Chief with me and constantly remain in contact so that he could not entertain other thoughts. When martial law is declared, he will, as martial law commander, handle the situation, so I had called him in advance to sever his contact with the outside and to verify the progress of the situation directly.”
(Same purport in the prosecutor’s record p. 10 and trial transcript pp. 197, 542)

2) “Q: Explain in detail the course of the assassination of the President.
A: ... On the same day, around 16:30, arriving at my office, ... lying down on the bed there, I was for a long time imagining what would happen after the act ... continuing to imagine ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 3-4; trial transcript p. 197 uses the phrase “revolutionary plan”)

3) “Q: Same as above.
A: At around 17:40, after hearing that C, the Chief Secretary of the Blue House, had arrived, I came down to the first floor and entered the reception room. The first words of Chief Secretary C were, ‘The Agency has had a hard time and the Republican Party fellows have ruined everything,’ so I said casually, ‘There is nothing we can do. From now on, when AY’s acting administration is launched, we will have to attach them one by one,’ and ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 4)

4) “Q: Same as above.
A: Sitting again with C on the curb at the right front gate of that entrance, continuing the conversation, after hearing Chief Secretary C say first, ‘That friend T, the chief, is so hard-line and troublesome. He listens only to one or two opposition-party fellows and rushes to report to the President,’ ... I had already resolved to remove the President and T ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 4-5; trial transcript p. 198 to the same effect)

5) “Q: Same as above.
A: ... Then, at around 18:50, the President and T arrived ... and dinner began ... The President asked me, ‘How is the New Democratic Party operation?’ so I said, ‘Because of the Republican Party announcement, everything has been ruined. The fellows who said they would resign have all turned hard-line. As far as I can see, it will be difficult for the AY acting administration system to be launched for the time being. The mainstreams have become hard-line, so it will be somewhat noisy.’”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 5)

6) “Q: But you departed for the Namsan Intelligence Agency. How did you enter Army Headquarters?
A: ... I took Chief Secretary C alone into the adjacent restroom ... and said, ‘You must remove the signboard of the Martial Law Command as soon as possible and change it to the Revolutionary Committee signboard.’”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 17-18)

7) “Then why did you also kill Chief Secretary T?
A: In order for me to carry out the act, I could only achieve the purpose by dealing together with the obstacle T and the escort officers. Taking these together with the other lawfully admitted evidence cited by the lower judgment, the above reasoning is fully understandable.

Meanwhile, Defendant A strongly argued in this respect that the so-called Yushin system, in its establishment and continuation, destroyed the political basic order of the democratic state, so this offense was solely for restoring democracy. His explanation was gradually systematized as this case proceeded and, as well expressed in the supplemental statement of appeal grounds submitted by Defendant A himself, appears fairly persuasive.

However, it is acknowledged that the current Constitution contains some non-democratic provisions as pointed out in the argument, but the current Constitution also declares that our country is a democratic republic and that sovereignty resides in the people, provides for the fundamental rights of the people including the guarantee of human rights, and is unquestionably a democratic constitution in its essence, with separation of the three powers. Therefore, the argument that the Yushin Constitution itself usurped sovereignty or destroyed the political basic order of the democratic state and that it itself was a state of insurrection is excessively exaggerated and merely dogmatic, having no value for consideration. Moreover, as to the claim that the offense was for restoring democracy, this is plainly fictitious from the circumstances noted above. We further examine this point using the evidence lawfully cited in the lower judgment.

(3) Therefore, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. As noted above, it cannot be said that the Defendants, in this offense, lacked conclusive awareness or conditional awareness of unlawfully destroying the political basic order prescribed by the present Constitution or laws, and it cannot be said that they merely killed a natural person who was a specific constitutional organ. Nor can it be said that the purpose was not direct; moreover, in the case of Defendant A, the post-offense formation of a government was also specifically planned.

Accordingly, since no illegality alleged in the appeal is found in the lower judgment, all arguments are without merit.

(4) However, with respect to this point, Supreme Court Justices Min Mun-gi and Yang Byeong-ho have separate opinions concerning all six Defendants, Justice Seo Yun-hong has a separate opinion concerning Defendants C, E, F, and G, and Justices Im Hang-jun and Jeong Tae-won have separate opinions concerning Defendants E, F, and G, as set forth in Section 11 below.

2. 「폭동」

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the insurrectionary act under Article 87 of the Criminal Act is punished according to the degree of participation in the riot when the act was committed for the prescribed purpose. In such case, riot means a combination of a number of persons with some organization that uses violence or intimidation to the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, and such riot must bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. However, first, the Defendants in this case cannot be said to constitute a combination of a number of persons with any organization; second, it cannot be found at all that they used the above violence or intimidation, nor did they reach the degree of disturbing the peace of a locality; and third, although the Defendants’ acts as found by the judgment below cannot be said to bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of subverting the Constitution, the lower court recognized the facts as found and punished them for murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection. It is argued that this constitutes misinterpretation of law concerning riot in the crime of insurrection, violation of the rules of evidence, and failure of hearing. We consider this argument.

Upon review, riot as an element of Article 87 of the Criminal Act means a number of persons combining to commit violence or intimidation. In such case, the combination of many persons requires some degree of organization, but the number cannot be specified. Also, the degree of violence or intimidation must be such as to disturb the peace of a locality; when that degree is reached, the offense is consummated, and when it is not reached, it becomes an attempt.

Further, as argued, the riot must, of course, bear a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. In this case, even when reviewing the evidence lawfully cited by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. In this offense, initially, the leader Defendant A sequentially combined with E and F, and Defendant D with E, and E with G, and so on, as is clear from the lower court’s reasoning. That is enough to constitute a number of persons for the execution of a riot. And according to Defendant A’s initial intention, to achieve the purpose of subverting the Constitution in this case, Defendant C was to be brought in as a cooperating force, the Army Chief of Staff was to be drawn in by persuasion or intimidation, and the extensive organizational power of the Central Intelligence Agency was to be used. The above Defendants easily combined based on their positions, trust, and personal relationships as recognized from the record, and their division of roles was clearly determined, so it may be recognized as organized. The gunfire described in the lower judgment constitutes violence or intimidation as riot. Whether the gunfire after that also provides material to view it as a riot is considered in item 5 below. However, it cannot be said that this reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, though the lower court also held it to be an attempt on the same grounds. On the other hand, according to the record, some of the Defendants were preparing for a gun battle with the Blue House security guards after the above gunfire, and further clashes between military units due to cooperation or opposition were anticipated; if it had come to that, it would undoubtedly have been sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality. In light of the purpose to subvert the Constitution discussed above, it cannot be denied that the riot in this case bore a means-end relationship to the purpose of insurrection. Meanwhile, the lower judgment found and punished Defendant C as an attempted major participant in the insurrection, and Article 87(2) of the Criminal Act defines a major participant broadly to include, for example, those responsible for supply, accounting, liaison, communications, sanitation, general affairs, and similar duties. Defendant C’s original mission falls within a major role in this insurrection case, and it is possible for such a major role to involve no violence or intimidation at all.

Therefore, since no illegality alleged in the appeal is found in the lower judgment, all arguments are without merit.

However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng have separate opinions concerning all six Defendants, and Justices Yang Byeong-ho and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions concerning Defendant C, as set forth in Section 11 below. Also, ex officio, although it is recognized that the lower court properly treated the acts of Defendants A, D, E, F, and G as imaginary concurrence between murder with insurrectionary purpose and attempted insurrection, there are differing opinions by Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, and Kim Yun-haeng on this point.

3. 「가담」

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that Defendant C was not in a hierarchical superior-subordinate status with Defendant A as a state official and thus cannot be said to have joined a group for carrying out the insurrectionary acts in this case. Moreover, there was no conspiratorial agreement regarding mutual communication in the group for carrying out insurrection. Nevertheless, the lower court held that Defendant C joined the group when he received instructions from Defendant A, the leader, to keep security, as if he had joined the group. This, it is argued, was a fact-finding without evidence, or there was a failure of hearing and contradiction in reasons, and it violated the Supreme Court precedent on co-principal liability. We consider this argument.

Upon review, as determined in the above items, Defendant C also clearly participated in this insurrection. Reviewing the evidence lawfully cited by the lower court in light of the record, one can recognize Defendant C’s original acts concerning attempted major participation in insurrection, namely security maintenance, prohibition of troop movement from the Blue House, recommendation of martial law declaration, etc., and these were indispensable for carrying out the insurrectionary acts in this case. As such, they themselves provide important factual material for the alleged participation, and considering the evidence cited by the lower court, the lower court’s factual findings on this point are proper. The fact that Defendant C was not in the hierarchical status alleged vis-à-vis Defendant A, the leader, cannot be said to obstruct the above factual findings. Also, as expressed in Defendant A’s statement to the prosecutor that after the assassination of the President, “please explain in detail the course of the suspect’s conduct after that,” and Defendant A said, “Immediately thereafter, as I came out onto the floor, I encountered Chief Secretary C standing there, and when I said, ‘I will do it if I do it. It is all over now. Please keep security tight,’ Chief Secretary C asked back, ‘What did you say?’ so I said, ‘You should say that the President fainted from overwork, or say something appropriate,’ and Chief Secretary C answered, ‘Anyway, I understand,’ so I thought Chief Secretary C had completely understood,” Defendant C cannot be said not to have had sufficient communication of intent with Defendant A while agreeing to perform the original mission. Therefore, the lower judgment contains no illegality alleged in the appeal, and this argument also lacks merit.

However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions.

4. 「살해」

Among the Grounds of Appeal, in light of the record in this case, the deceased T’s gunshot wound, inflicted by Defendant A’s gunfire progressing from the front of the right shoulder joint toward the lower left, was a fatal wound; and Defendant G fired two shots only after T had already died. Also, the deceased U died from fatal gunshot wounds to the front of the right chest wall and the right scapular area, causing cardiac injury and death by cardiac tamponade; afterward, Defendant G fired one shot causing a blind-ended wound to the right buttock, which had no relation to U’s fatal injury. Nevertheless, the lower judgment found Defendant G guilty and punished him for the offense of murder with insurrectionary purpose. It is argued that this violated the rules of evidence by finding facts of killing without evidence or misunderstood the legal principles of murder. We consider this argument.

According to the reasoning of the lower judgment, the lower court recognized as to Defendant G responsibility for the killing of two of the six deceased persons in this case, T and U. According to the entries in the autopsy reports and on-site inspection report for T and U in the investigation record, the deceased T had wounds: ㉮ blind-ended wound to the front of the right shoulder joint, ㉯ blind-ended wound to the left abdomen, ㉰ blind-ended wound to the left flank, and ㉱ through-and-through wound of the right wrist; among these, the gunshot wound located centrally at the right shoulder joint was the fatal wound, believed to have been caused by a small-caliber pistol shot. The deceased U had wounds: ㉮ blind-ended wound to the front of the right chest wall, ㉯ blind-ended wound to the lateral left chest wall, ㉰ blind-ended wound to the lower left chest wall, ㉱ blind-ended wound to the right scapular area, ㉲ blind-ended wound to the right buttock, and ㉳ through-and-through wound at the right iliac crest; among these, the gunshot wound to the front of the right chest wall and the gunshot wound to the right scapular area were fatal wounds, and it is presumed that he fell because of them. Thus, parts of the record support the argument. However, among the various lawfully admitted pieces of evidence cited by the lower court, the following appear:

(1) Defendant C’s statements
(a) “Q: Then state the circumstances by which you came to conduct the confirmation killing.
A: Following E into the room, I fired one shot at a person lying at the entrance to the security guards’ waiting room, and then two shots at a person lying face down on the opposite side of the waiting room. At that time, I heard a groaning sound of ‘ugh’ from the banquet hall side, and after firing one shot at the fat person (Security Guard U) lying on his back with his face toward the sky, AJ, AK, AL, etc. were lying face down ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 224; however, at pp. 375 and 1450, he says he did not hear that groaning sound and did not see the left hand move)

(b) “Q: As to Chief of the Security Service T, did you not shoot him knowing perfectly well that he was still alive?
A: Yes, that is correct.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 225)

(2) Defendant C’s statements
“Explain in detail the course by which A assassinated T and the President.
A: ... Immediately afterward, curious, I entered the room used as the banquet hall, and while someone was looking into the room holding a pistol, I heard the words ‘T is not dead yet’ ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 49; trial transcript p. 258)

(3) Defendant E’s statements
(a) “Q: State the circumstances from the shooting of the President’s guards, etc. up to the point where the President was taken to the hospital.
A: ... When I looked into the banquet room, I saw two legs, so I cried ‘don’t move,’ and looked inside, where Chief of Security Cha Chi-cheol was lying with his eyes open, and it seemed that his hand was still moving ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 180-181; trial transcript p. 356)

(b) “Q: When you told D that the President had been injured and gone to the hospital, what did you talk about?
A: When I said he had been transported, the person inside asked, ‘How is it?’ so I thought he was talking about Chief T, and when I said, ‘I’m not sure whether he was injured or dead,’ he seemed to speak to G and said to clean it up completely.”
(Trial transcript p. 504)

(4) Statement of first-instance witness AS
(a) “Q: Was Chief of Security T there?
A: As I was trying to get out of there, the chief of security was by the door, so I tried to help him up, but he said he did not think he could get up, so I just went out. AI guided me to a side room, and I kept hearing groaning sounds from somewhere ...”
(Trial transcript p. 577)

(b) “Q: Did you touch Chief T’s body or look at him carefully?
A: I looked at his face and touched only his hand. It seemed he was waving by the door, so I touched his hand, and when I tried to help him up, he said, ‘I don’t think I can get up.’”
(Trial transcript p. 586)

(5) Statement of first-instance witness AI
“Q: Did you see Chief T lying down at that time?
A: I saw him. After I carried the President out, I saw him lying on the left side.
Q: What was Chief T saying then?
A: I do not know whether he saw me, but he was calling ‘AZ, AZ.’
Q: So what did you do?
A: At that time, as I was coming out with the female guest next to me, I tried to help him up ...”
(Trial transcript p. 663)

(6) Statement of first-instance witness AJ
(a) “Q: Then did you hear groaning sounds from U and Lee Jeong-o?
A: ... Hearing cries of ‘Aigoo, aigoo,’ I saw that it was Security Guard U.”
(Trial transcript pp. 666-667)

(b) “Q: Judging from the location where he was lying in the kitchen at that time, who would have been the first person to catch the eye of someone coming from the living room?
A: Security Guard U.”
(Trial transcript p. 667)

(c) Statement of first-instance witness AK
“Q: What did the fat security guard say at that time?
A: He said, ‘Save me.’
Q: Was he groaning until before G fired?
A: Yes, before he fired.”
(Trial transcript p. 691)

Taking these together with the other lawfully admitted evidence cited by the lower judgment, it can be sufficiently recognized from the record that T and U were alive until immediately before the shock caused by Defendant G’s action and were completely killed by that gunfire. In murder, the object is a living person, and whether the victim had the capacity to survive is irrelevant. Where independent acts clearly caused the result of death, there is no inconsistency in punishing each act as a consummated offense. Therefore, no illegality such as alleged can be found in the lower court’s factual findings or reasoning process. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.

However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Im Hang-jun, Jeong Tae-won, and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions.

5. 내란의 execution commencement 및 consummation 시기

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the crime of insurrection becomes consummated when a riot is initiated for the purpose of subverting the Constitution and the riot reaches consummation, regardless of whether the purpose of subverting the Constitution has been attained. In this case, if the President, his chief of security, and the escort guards were murdered for the purpose of subverting the Constitution, that would amount to a riot sufficient to disturb the peace of a locality, and the crime of insurrection would have reached consummation regardless of whether the constitutional-subversion purpose was achieved. Therefore, Defendant C’s conduct in this insurrection is a post-offense act not punishable, or otherwise the execution had not yet commenced. Nevertheless, the lower court found Defendant C guilty of attempted major participation in insurrection. It is argued that the lower court misunderstood the legal principles concerning the commencement of execution and consummation of the crime of insurrection, or committed violations of the rules of evidence and contradiction in reasons. We consider this argument.

Upon review, it is true, as argued, that the crime of insurrection may be consummated after the group action as a riot has begun, regardless of whether the purpose of territorial usurpation or subversion of the Constitution has been achieved. However, the riot must have reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality before consummation occurs. In this case, the riotous acts described in the lower judgment alone cannot be said to have reached the extent of disturbing the peace of a locality, so it is not proper to say that the crime of insurrection in this case was consummated. Further, as for the concept of violence or intimidation as riot conduct, this is the broadest possible concept, and the conduct of preparing for or assisting such acts is comprehensively understood as riot. In this case, the state of armed guarding by Defendant F pursuant to Defendant C’s instructions at the Seoul District Army Hospital, the state of surveillance by Central Intelligence Agency personnel who did not know what was happening at Namdaemun and Seoul Station pursuant to the instructions of the deceased Park Heung-ju, who was a first-instance defendant, and the state of waiting of security vehicles at Army Headquarters, together with the facts discernible from the record by other lawfully cited evidence of the lower judgment, namely: (i) the state of security guards at the Gungjeong-dong restaurant of the Central Intelligence Agency after the gunfire there, in preparation for the approach of Blue House security guards; (ii) the surveillance state of Defendant A, as in Defendant A’s prosecutor statement: “Q: If the Army Chief of Staff and the second assistant director of the Central Intelligence Agency did not listen, A: After the act, I would persuade them, bring them to the side of the revolution, and if they still did not listen, I would intimidate or detain them and make them follow as I intended. So I kept close by them and monitored them ...”; and the consciousness of Defendant A and C as in “Chief Secretary C hesitated a little on the phone, then said, ‘All right, I will go there’ (I felt at that time that Chief Secretary C thought I had taken the Army Chief as a hostage and was consenting),” collectively show that the riot did not end after the Gungjeong-dong restaurant gunfire but continued. In particular, Defendant G’s confirmation killing took place after Defendant C had participated in the insurrection, so it cannot be said that Defendant C merely participated in an unpunishable post-offense act. Also, the appellate court’s measure of regarding the riot as having commenced execution when the riotous act began is proper. Therefore, the lower judgment has no illegality such as alleged, and this argument lacks merit.

However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi and Yang Byeong-ho have separate opinions.

6. 「증거은닉」

Among the Grounds of Appeal, it is argued that, as the elements of the offense of concealment of evidence, only where the objective requirement that the evidence concern another person’s criminal or disciplinary case and the subjective requirement of intent to conceal it are satisfied can the act be punished. Yet Defendant H did not know that the items in question were evidence used in the offense of killing the former President and T’s party, and also had no intent whatsoever to conceal those items. Nevertheless, the lower court upheld the first-instance finding of guilt for concealment of evidence against Defendant H. It is argued that this violated the rules of evidence or constituted a failure of hearing or a misunderstanding of the legal principles concerning concealment of evidence. We consider this argument.

Upon review, it is true, as argued, that the offense of concealment of evidence is constituted when a person subjectively recognizes evidence relating to another person’s criminal or disciplinary case and conceals it. Reviewing the various pieces of evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court in light of the record:

(1) Defendant H:
(a) “I knew that the President had come to the banquet room while I was working as a guard at the scene of the offense.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 244; trial transcript p. 380)

(b) “Because gunshots kept sounding loudly from the banquet room side, I became anxious, and G suggested that we should do our own security, so I armed myself with an M16 rifle ... Shortly afterward, AK, the cook from the other building, entered with his face as white as paper, so when I asked what happened, he said the lights suddenly went out and shots were fired from all directions, and he was lying face down on the kitchen floor.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 245)

(c) In response to the question, “When did you know that President Park and the security guards had been killed in the shooting incident on the evening of October 26?”, he said: “The next day, around 05:00, while I was sleeping, I woke up and heard the news of the President’s absence from the radio in the waiting room in front of the room, and learned of it.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 243)

“I heard the news on October 27, 1979, around 05:00, that the President was absent and the Prime Minister would act, and I thought it would be a big matter if the President passed away.”
(Trial transcript p. 382)

“In response to the question whether he thought the above news was related to the gunshots of the previous day, he answered that because he heard the gunshots he thought it was related. Also, when asked what he understood the meaning of absence to be, he answered that he understood it to mean that he had died.”
(Trial transcript p. 441)

(d) “Regarding how I received the pistol, etc. from E, E gave me two pistols held in both hands and told me that there was aluminum foil in the kitchen, so I should wrap them in aluminum foil, take the shovel in the basement of the new building, and bury them somewhere in the garden.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 242)

(e) In response to the question of where he thought the guns had come from, he said: “The moment I received them from E, I thought they must be the ones used in the gun battle that had taken place in the old building of the guesthouse on the evening of October 26, but since I was told to do it, I carried it out as instructed.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 243)

(2) Defendant E stated: “Around 07:00, being concerned that the pistols and other items used in the offense might be discovered, I gave the guard H the pistol I had placed in the desk drawer and the security guard’s pistol hidden under the blanket, and ordered him to go into the kitchen, wrap them in aluminum foil, and bury them in the garden with the shovel in the basement.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 184)

Considering the other evidence together, the first-instance court’s factual finding and legal application regarding concealment of evidence as upheld by the lower court against Defendant H are proper, and it cannot be said that the rules of evidence were violated as alleged, or that there was a failure of hearing or misunderstanding of the legal principles. Therefore, this argument lacks merit.

Section 5. 살인죄의 공동정범 관련 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the lower court held that Defendant C conspired with Defendant A to kill T. However, co-principal liability is, in essence, based on two or more persons jointly, in mutual cooperation, executing their common criminal intent, and to commit a crime with the intention of acting jointly requires not only communication of intent but also a concrete disclosure of the contents, means, and method of that conspiracy. In addition, beyond such communication of intent, there must be a fact of joint execution as an objective constituent element. Further, in its original form co-principal liability is principally a form of execution co-principal liability, while conspiracy co-principal liability is a ceremonial form in which a person participates only in the conspiracy and does not perform the constituent facts at all, yet is held to the same criminal responsibility as the executor. It arose in actual judicial practice as a theory of accomplice liability where the substantive principal plans the crime behind the scenes and causes subordinates or persons under his control to carry out the execution, making it impossible to treat it as mere instigation or aiding and abetting. Therefore, mere awareness of the crime or communication of intent is insufficient; the word conspiracy means a fairly high degree of consultation such as discussing the execution of the crime and determining even the role of the executor. As to a conspirator who does not undertake the execution act, there must be a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor. In this case, the conversation or behavior between Defendants A and C in the garden at the restaurant cannot by itself be definitively taken as a proposal to commit murder jointly or as assent thereto, and even the lower court’s explanation cannot be taken to imply that there was intent to kill or communication of such intent; nor is there evidence to support it. Moreover, Defendant C, unlike Defendant A, did not share the execution role when Defendant A killed the chief of security; rather, it appears that he attempted to restrain Defendant A from committing murder. Nevertheless, the lower court recognized Defendant C as a co-principal in the offense of murder and punished him accordingly. In any event, this is far removed from Defendant C’s explanation or Defendant A’s statements. It is argued that the lower court thus found facts without evidence, violated the rules of evidence, and committed a defect for lack of reasons and failure of hearing; and further, it misunderstood the law concerning co-principal liability and omission crimes. We consider this argument.

Upon review, since the lower court clearly applied conspiracy co-principal liability to Defendant C concerning the murder of the deceased T, there is no need to consider further the arguments premised on execution co-principal liability. It is a precedent of this Court that in co-principal liability, even if one does not directly participate in the execution after conspiring to commit the offense, one cannot avoid co-principal liability for the acts carried out by other co-conspirators. In conspiracy co-principal liability, conspiracy means communication of intent among two or more persons to cooperate and realize their common criminal intent. As argued, the conspirator who does not undertake the execution act must have a subjective intent to realize his own crime through the executor; of course, but it is not necessarily required that he be the substantive principal behind the scenes who plans the crime and causes a subordinate or controllable person to carry it out.

In this case, reviewing the evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court in light of the record, the lower court’s factual findings and reasoning on this point are proper. However, if one quotes the important evidence recognized from the record:

1. Defendant C’s statements

(1) “Q: Explain in detail your relationship with T while you were serving as chief secretary.
A: ... I was displeased with Chief T’s overbearing conduct. As to me, since I had taken office as chief secretary on December 22, 1978, ... ① not long after that, although I formally visited T’s office to pay my respects on assuming office, T never returned the visit, which I found insulting. Also, ② when I was going to report to him, etiquette required that he come upstairs to my office if he had something to say, but instead T always had a guard call me down to the first-floor waiting room, and I felt that T was somewhat arrogant and too strong in personality ... T had such a strong sense of authority that during his tenure he never even once came to my office. And ③ when the President inspected the Government Complex or attended meetings and used the guest elevator ... T would sometimes tell me to use a different elevator that was waiting. ② Even in work reporting matters, I ordinarily would receive approval immediately with the documents if the President came to work each day, but T would wait in the office before the President arrived and go in first to report, interfering with my obtaining approval, or when I or a minister was waiting to receive approval, T would contact the guard at the entrance to the President’s office and instruct him not to let me in because he had business to see the President, making me wait and then going in to report first ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 36-39; trial transcript pp. 240-241 to the same effect)

(2) “Q: Same as above.
A: ... T also frequently engaged in abuses of authority by involving himself in political operation matters that were not even his work, collecting intelligence and reporting it to the President ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 39; trial transcript p. 240 to the same effect)

(3) “Q: Same as above.
A: ... In addition, he was arrogant and rude even toward me, an elder, ministers, the Speaker of the National Assembly, or senior military figures, never adding the honorific ‘nim’ when addressing anyone ... In light of these points, my relationship with T was one that could not coexist, and I was thinking of having him step down by making a proposal to the President someday.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 40; trial transcript p. 241 to the same effect)

(4) “Q: State, to the best of your knowledge, the relationship between T, the chief of the security service, and A.
A: ... After being scolded by the President for ... the reason, A noticed that it was due to T’s manipulation and his anger reached the extreme.”

(5) “Q: From when did you and A start criticizing T together, and what was the content?
A: From about two months after I objected, and whenever I met A, it was mainly about T’s arrogant and rude behavior and especially that he was deeply involved in political matters and, with hard-line statements and proposals only, caused the President to hesitate in his decisions.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 43; trial transcript p. 243 to the same effect)

(6) “Q: What did you talk about with Bureau Chief Kim after arriving at Gungjeong-dong?
A: When I said, ‘A fellow like a thing sitting in clear water and constantly muddying the water—how can work be done? We should get that fellow (meaning T) today ...,’ I said, ‘He listens to only one or two of the opposition fellows and rushes over to tell the President, and he’s hard-line and troublesome,’ and when Bureau Chief Kim said, ‘Shall we take that fellow out today?,’ I just nodded silently ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 45; however, at trial transcript pp. 247 and 1391 he denies it)

(7) “Q: ... When A said, ‘Please take care of what happens after this, brother,’ what did it mean when you nodded your head?
A: It was agreement to remove T, because A and T were usually extremely ill-disposed toward each other, and I too always had dissatisfaction with T. As to the words ‘please take care of it,’ I thought that if you explained well to the President and made the President understand A’s true intention, A’s life at least could be saved, so I agreed.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 63; at trial transcript p. 249 he states that he did say something like that during the prosecutor’s investigation)

(8) “Q: What was your state of mind when A left the banquet table?
A: ... As time passed ... A’s gloomy expression and the conversation held in front of the entrance ... came to mind ... and it is true that I felt uneasy and impatient.”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 64-65; however, at trial transcript p. 254 he denies the purport)

(9) “Q: When A ... tapped your side, what did you think?
A: ... I thought at last that something big was happening.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 65)

(10) “Q: What did you hear from A in the restroom of the banka office of the Army Chief of Staff?
A: As soon as I went in, I said to A, ‘How could you do that even to the President?’ ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 75; on this point Defendant A’s statements also coincide)

2. Defendant A’s statements

(1) “Q: What was your relationship with former Blue House Security Chief T?
A: It is true that T, beyond his proper duty of security work, intruded into political matters and other broad affairs and had hard-line positions in opinions and assertions, so I constantly thought of him as objectionable. Also, even though T was a junior officer and younger than me, he would sometimes offend me by arrogant and rude behavior toward me or elders.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 22)

(2) “Q: State, to the best of your knowledge, the ordinary relationship between Chief C and Security Chief T.
A: Two or three weeks after Chief C took office, I visited the chief’s office and heard him vent his dissatisfaction with Chief T, saying ‘I’ll have to settle this with that guy or find some way,’ and thereafter I several times heard him express great dissatisfaction due to disagreements and trivial disputes with Chief T ... I can conclusively say that the relationship between the two was not fundamentally a good one.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 30; trial transcript pp. 199-200 to the same effect, and at the time he is said to have said, “When a colonel and a captain fight, you must scold the colonel, so please endure it.”)

(3) “Q: Explain in detail the course of the assassination of the President.
A: ... When I looked at Chief C’s expression while saying, ‘Shall I get rid of that guy?,’ he kept nodding, so I understood that he agreed; then when I said, ‘Please take care of what happens after this, brother,’ he again nodded, and I understood that he was agreeing ...”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 5; however, at trial transcript pp. 199, 542, 1510, etc., this is partly denied)

(4) “Q: Have you been accustomed to saying ‘get rid of him’ as a habit?
A: As far as I remember, saying that I would get rid of Chief T was the first time that day.”
(Trial transcript p. 542)

(5) “Q: What if Chief C had objected to your proposal to eliminate T?
A: I would have just brushed it off by saying it was a joke, and I would have died together at the scene of the President’s assassination.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 11; trial transcript p. 200 to the same effect)

In light of this, it cannot be said that there was no communication of intent between Defendant C and Defendant A to cooperate and jointly realize the intent to kill the deceased T. Nor can it be said that Defendant C had no intent to realize his own murderous intent toward T through Defendant A. In particular, Defendant A’s act of accepting the imminent timing of the offense as described above and his act of leaving the scene during the gunfire can be viewed as aiding acts for Defendant A’s criminal execution. Therefore, the lower court’s factual findings and reasoning on this point are all proper, and there is no illegality such as alleged. Accordingly, this argument lacks merit.

However, on this point, Justices Min Mun-gi, Yang Byeong-ho, Im Hang-jun, Kim Yun-haeng, and Seo Yun-hong have separate opinions as set forth in Section 11 below.

Section 6. 중지미수에 관한 위법

Among the Grounds of Appeal, the lower court’s holding, in relation to attempted major participation in insurrection against Defendant C, that the facts of “opposition by the Prime Minister and the Ministers of Home Affairs and Justice” cannot necessarily be said to constitute the reason for the failure of the insurrection, and that the fact of “pressure by Blue House Chief Secretary Z” cannot be said to be a decisive obstacle to insurrection, and in addition there is no evidence to support these points, whereas in fact Defendant C, if he had wanted to help Defendant A after 23:00 that day, could have done so, but instead it was clear that he had him arrested of his own accord. Nevertheless, the lower court found him guilty of attempted major participation in insurrection. It is argued that there was a violation of the rules of evidence, failure of hearing, and misunderstanding of the law concerning abandonment of attempt, and also that the lower court failed to determine the defense on the above purport and thus committed a defect for lack of reasons. We consider this argument.

Upon review, if the various pieces of evidence lawfully admitted by the lower court are examined in light of the record, the lower court’s action on this point is proper. Therefore, the above argument is plainly without merit. However, if one identifies the important basis of the lower court’s measure below:

1. Defendant C’s prosecutor statement

(1) “Q: Explain in detail the words exchanged and atmosphere at the Minister of National Defense’s office.
A: Around 21:40 that day, at the Minister of National Defense’s office ... when I said to the Prime Minister, ‘If you are going to declare emergency martial law, shouldn’t you convene the cabinet meeting?’ he said, ‘Of course,’ and then asked, ‘What shall we state as the reason for martial law? Shall we say the President has passed away? Shall we say he is absent?’ So I said, ‘If we say emergency martial law is declared from 00:00 on the 27th due to the President’s absence, wouldn’t that do?’ But the Prime Minister said, ‘Would the public accept it if we say only absence? You need to say some reason the public can accept; the cabinet ministers must know some substance in order to exchange opinions, must they not?’ Then A, who was beside us, objected saying, ‘Absence won’t do. It must be stated that martial law is being declared because the domestic security situation is bad.’ The Prime Minister objected, saying, ‘There were no demonstrations in the country, and Busan, where martial law has been declared, is quiet, so we cannot use such a reason; how can we keep the President’s absence from the public? It will be difficult to maintain secrecy all the way, and first the cabinet ministers will not accept it.’ Then A said, ‘Why not? The Soviet Union did not announce AD’s movements for over a week, so why can’t we keep secrecy for two or three days?’ When the Prime Minister said, ‘Then can Bureau Chief Kim or Chief Secretary C explain the reason at the cabinet meeting?’, A said, ‘Yes, I can,’ but I objected, saying, ‘That will not do. We are not cabinet ministers, so we cannot enter.’”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 55-57; trial transcript pp. 269 and following to the same effect)

(2) “Q: How did you feel in the atmosphere at that time?
A: Yes, I felt that the cabinet ministers were showing a rather strong reaction, stronger than I had expected.”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 57-58)

(3) “Q: What was the attitude of the cabinet ministers at that time?
A: My thought that, as expected, the cabinet ministers had come under A’s control and were within his sphere of influence was completely mistaken, because I got the impression that the cabinet ministers were reacting against A’s assertions.”
(Prosecutor’s record p. 76)

2. Defendant A’s prosecutor statement

(1) “Q: After going up to the Ministry of National Defense, what did you do?
A: I was inside the Minister of National Defense’s office ... Chief Secretary C was seated with me ... The chief secretary Z said, ‘As I was coming, reporters were gathered near the Government Complex and seem to have noticed something,’ so I instructed Assistant Vice-Director AH to strictly control domestic reporting and to tell Assistant Director AM to control any foreign reporters so that they would not notice and send out reports ...”
(Prosecutor’s record pp. 18-19)

(2) “Q: After going up to the Ministry of National Defense, what did you do?
A: ... When the Minister of Culture and Public Information asked, ‘We should inform the public of the reason for the martial law declaration, but what shall we announce?’, I said, ‘Wouldn’t it be enough to say only that an emergency situation has arisen in the country and martial law is being declared?’ Then the Prime Minister said, ‘We have to give cabinet ministers an explanatory statement for the declaration of emergency martial law, so what shall we say?’ ... After much back and forth we could not reach a conclusion, and at around 23:30 the Prime Minister said, ‘Please have Chief Secretary C attend the cabinet meeting and explain.’ Chief Secretary C said, ‘Prime Minister, please do it.
