1) Non-Indicted Person 3, as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, which was the criminal facts giving rise to the voluntary submission, voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive during the investigation against him. The instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein are evidence not only concerning the suspected facts of Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., who are the principal offenders, but also the direct object of the concealment act, and thus constitute evidence concerning Non-Indicted Person 3’s suspicion of concealment of evidence. Accordingly, Non-Indicted Person 3 is a person with a substantive interest in the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein. Throughout the entire process, including the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive itself and the searching, copying, and printing of the electronic information related to the suspicion of concealment of evidence, Non-Indicted Person 3 has an interest in participation.

2) As the investigation into himself and Non-Indicted Persons 2, etc. became full-scale, Non-Indicted Person 1 delivered the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 while instructing him to hide it. Non-Indicted Person 3 voluntarily concealed the instant hard disk drive in a place known only to himself so that it would not be discovered. Thereafter, when Non-Indicted Person 3 was taken into custody as a suspect on suspicion of concealment of evidence, he disclosed the concealment to the law-enforcement agency and voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive. In light of the circumstances surrounding the concealment and voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, and the extent of involvement of Non-Indicted Person 3 and Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. in that process, it may be said that the person who actually possessed the instant hard disk drive at the time of seizure and search or at a time close thereto was Non-Indicted Person 3. Further, insofar as Non-Indicted Person 3 actually possessed the instant hard disk drive around that time by the foregoing circumstances, it may be regarded, absent other special circumstances, that he was also in a position to de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of the stored electronic information.

3) Non-Indicted Person 1 was not the suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, which was the criminal facts giving rise to the voluntary submission, and moreover, he delivered the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3, requesting vaguely that it be hidden “until the investigation into himself is over,” with the purpose of concealing the very existence of the instant hard disk drive. This can be regarded as an expression of an intention, under the purpose of concealing and severing the outward connection between himself and the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein, to abandon or wholly transfer to Non-Indicted Person 3 the exclusive right of domination and control over the instant hard disk drive until the indefinite time of “completion of the investigation,” if necessary for achieving that purpose. As a result, Non-Indicted Person 3 came to be in a state where he could de facto retain and exercise actual and factual domination over the instant hard disk drive and exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information stored therein, and he actually exercised that authority by concealing the instant hard disk drive at a place of his own choosing and thereafter voluntarily submitting it to the law-enforcement agency.

2. Determination of the remaining arguments for final appeal

The lower court maintained the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case guilty for the reasons stated in the opinion. Examining the reasons of the lower-court judgment in light of the relevant legal principles and the evidence duly admitted, there is no error affecting the judgment in that the lower court either exceeded the limits of free evaluation of evidence by violating the rules of logic and experience, without fully conducting the necessary examination, or misunderstood the legal principles concerning relevance between the seized items and the facts charged, abuse of prosecutorial authority, the presumption of innocence and the principle of trial based on evidence concerning the falsity of the instant certificate, deception and risk of result in the crime of obstruction of business, intent and co-principal liability, and the admissibility of derivative evidence, etc.

3. Conclusion

Therefore, the final appeal is dismissed, and judgment is rendered as stated in the main text. In this judgment, except for the dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justices Min Yu-sook, Lee Heung-gu, and Oh Kyung-mi, the views of the participating Justices were unanimous, and there are the concurring opinions of Supreme Court Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion, as well as the concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justice Oh Kyung-mi on the dissenting opinion.

4. Dissenting opinion of Supreme Court Justices Min Yu-sook, Lee Heung-gu, and Oh Kyung-mi

a. Summary of the dissenting opinion

1) The majority opinion held that Non-Indicted Person 3, who voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive, had a substantive interest in the electronic information stored therein as a suspect in the offense of concealment of evidence, and could de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of that electronic information by actually possessing it; therefore, it was sufficient that participation rights were guaranteed to him in the seizure and search procedure, and since Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., who handed over the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 to conceal evidence concerning their own suspected facts, had abandoned or transferred the exclusive authority to manage and dispose of it, they did not correspond to the substantive persons subject to seizure who were the objects of the guarantee of participation rights.

2) However, we cannot agree. The majority opinion understands the “substantive person subject to seizure,” the subject to whom the participation right is guaranteed, narrowly with a focus on the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search, and this does not accord with the purport and direction of the precedents. In addition, according to the majority opinion, by disregarding the constitutional demand to realize due process and the principle of warrant requirement in the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning electronic information, which is increasingly important to individuals and businesses in modern society, it allows an anti-constitutional result in which the fundamental rights concerning the secrecy and freedom of private life of the electronic-information manager and disposer, who is the substantive person subject to seizure, are infringed.

3) In the above Supreme Court en banc decision 2016DO348 (hereinafter referred to as the “2016DO348 en banc decision”) and Supreme Court decision 2021DO11170, etc., the Supreme Court stated that the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the subject to whom participation rights are guaranteed in the seizure and search of electronic information, is a person who actually dominates and controls the digital storage medium concerned, retains and exercises exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in that digital storage medium, and can be evaluated as a person who is a substantive party to the seizure and search thereof. According to the legal principles and purport of such precedents, where, in addition to the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium, who is the direct party to the coercive disposition and the formal person subject to seizure, there separately exists an owner/manager, and there is a risk that his or her privacy and freedom, the right to informational self-determination, property rights, etc. concerning the electronic information may be infringed by the coercive disposition, that owner/manager must be regarded as the substantive person subject to seizure who is the object of the guarantee of participation rights. At this time, it is not required that the substantive person subject to seizure be the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search.

4) Therefore, where a person who concealed evidence received instruction from the principal offender to conceal evidence and voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency, in the status of a suspect, the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender that the evidence concealer had possessed and kept, and where the principal offender can be assessed as having a substantive interest not to have his privacy and freedom, etc. infringed during the search, copying, and printing of the electronic information stored in that digital storage medium, participation rights must also be guaranteed to the principal offender, who has such substantive interest together with the evidence concealer as both the voluntary submitter and the suspect.

On that point, we differ from the majority opinion. The detailed grounds are as follows.

b. The purport of guaranteeing participation rights in the seizure and search of electronic information and the concretization of the participation right

The participation-right doctrine in the seizure and search of electronic information in precedent evolved toward protecting the person who actually suffers infringement of fundamental rights, etc. by the coercive disposition, namely the substantive party to the seizure and search disposition, centering on the person subject to seizure who became the direct object of the State’s coercive disposition.

1) The Supreme Court first set forth, in its decision of May 26, 2011, 2009MO1190, the legal doctrine guaranteeing the participation right to the person subject to seizure or that person’s defense counsel in the seizure and search of the digital storage medium located in the office of the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union, which was the object of the coercive disposition. Subsequently, through the en banc decision of July 16, 2015, 2011MO1839, the Supreme Court reaffirmed, in the seizure and search of Kyungdong Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., the legal doctrine of guaranteeing participation rights centered on the person subject to seizure, who is the object of the coercive disposition, and declared that, where there is procedural illegality excluding the person subject to seizure’s participation right, the admissibility of evidence is, in principle, excluded.

In the above Supreme Court decisions 2009MO1190 and 2011MO1839 en banc, the Supreme Court emphasized that, although the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union and Kyungdong Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. were not in the status of suspects, they were in the status of persons subject to seizure who had a substantive interest not to have their right to informational self-determination, property rights, etc. infringed by the seizure and search of the law-enforcement agency, and recognized them as the subjects to whom participation rights belong. Thereafter, in various cases where the person subject to seizure and the suspect were the same person, the Supreme Court recognized the participation right in the person subject to seizure who was the object of the seizure and search disposition regarding the digital storage medium (see Supreme Court decisions of September 21, 2017, 2015DO12400; November 14, 2017, 2017DO3449; July 11, 2019, 2018DO20504, etc.), and finally, through the 2016DO348 en banc decision, held that where a coercive disposition is made against a digital storage medium owned and controlled by the suspect by making a third party the person subject to seizure when the person subject to seizure and the suspect are not the same person, appropriate measures must be taken, such as guaranteeing the participation right to the suspect who is the substantive person subject to seizure and delivering an inventory of the seized electronic information, thereby expanding the subject to whom the participation right is guaranteed to the substantive person subject to seizure. In Supreme Court decision of May 31, 2022, 2016MO587, while the law-enforcement agency conducted a seizure and search of the KakaoTalk conversation contents, etc. of the service user (suspect) stored on the server of the Internet service company Kakao Corp. by making Kakao Corp., the Internet service company, the person subject to seizure, the Supreme Court recognized the status of the service user as the substantive person subject to seizure, i.e. the subject to whom the participation right belongs. Meanwhile, in the above Supreme Court decision 2021DO11170, it was held that where a third party voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency a digital storage medium used by the suspect, if it can be seen that the authority to manage and dispose of it had been transferred to the third party, it is sufficient that the opportunity to participate was afforded to the third party who is not the suspect (the voluntary submitter).

2) Thus, the fact that the Supreme Court established the concept of participation rights centering on the “person subject to seizure” in the procedure for seizure and search of electronic information, and extended the subject to whom such rights belong to the substantive person subject to seizure, is the result of responding to the constitutional demand that, because in large-capacity computer or server information-processing systems, smartphones, and other digital storage media widely used in the work of corporations or individuals today, electronic information about private daily life or corporate management unrelated to criminal suspicion (hereinafter referred to as “irrelevant information”) is extensively intermingled with electronic information concerning the suspected facts subject to seizure (hereinafter referred to as “relevant information”), procedural measures are urgently needed to prevent the law-enforcement agency conducting coercive dispositions such as seizure and search from searching, copying, and printing irrelevant information as well, in order to protect the legal interests concerning the privacy and freedom of private life, the right to informational self-determination, property rights, etc. of individuals and businesses in this regard.

In this purport, the Supreme Court declared that, when a third party voluntarily submits a digital storage medium owned and controlled by the suspect, the object of seizure should be construed more narrowly to relevant information, because “the digital storage medium stores everything concerning personality-related legal interests such as the secrecy and freedom of private life and the right to informational self-determination, and considering that, even though the subject of the voluntary submission is merely a possessor or custodian other than the owner, if seizure and search are permitted without any restriction, there is a risk that the suspect’s personality-related legal interests will be substantially infringed, in cases where the submission act is likely to substantially infringe the owner’s privacy and other personality-related legal interests, special consideration for the legal interests of the owner who did not consent to the voluntary submission is required, together with the necessity of seizure and search pursuant to the voluntary submission” (see 2016DO348 en banc decision; Supreme Court decision of November 25, 2021, 2019DO7342, etc.).

c. The meaning of the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the subject to whom the participation right belongs, and the criteria for determining it

The substantive person subject to seizure who becomes the subject to whom the participation right belongs in the seizure and search of electronic information should be understood as a person who, until the time of seizure and search, actually dominates and manages the relevant digital storage medium while retaining and exercising exclusive authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in the digital storage medium, and who has personality-related legal interests, such as the secrecy and freedom of private life, that exclude the law-enforcement agency’s search and printing, etc. of irrelevant information intermingled with the digital storage medium with the information lawfully subject to seizure.

1) Participation right of the person subject to seizure, who is the object of coercive disposition

It is sufficient that the subject to whom the participation right belongs is the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium, etc. that became the object of the coercive disposition and the manager and disposer of the stored electronic information, that is, the real counterparty to the coercive disposition; it is not necessary that such person be the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search.

a) The Constitution of Korea provides that “no one shall be subjected to … seizure or search … except by due process of law” (the latter sentence of Article 12(1)), and that “when arresting, detaining, seizing, or searching, a warrant issued by a judge upon the request of a prosecutor in accordance with due process of law shall be presented” (the main text of Article 12(3)), thereby declaring the principles of due process of law and warrant requirement concerning seizure and search. In order to concretely realize due process of law and the principle of warrant requirement in seizure and search, the Criminal Procedure Act has established detailed provisions limiting the seizure and search procedure of the law-enforcement agency, such as the method of issuance of a seizure and search warrant, presentation of the warrant in the execution procedure, participation of the party and prior notice to the person with participation rights, and participation of the person in charge (Articles 219, 114, 118, 121, 122, and 123). In particular, Article 215(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “when necessary for criminal investigation, a prosecutor may, only insofar as there are circumstances from which the suspect may be deemed to have committed a crime and only with respect to those recognized as related to the relevant case, conduct seizure, search, or inspection by a warrant issued upon application to a judge of a district court,” thereby establishing the so-called “principle of relevance.”

The Supreme Court, focusing on the particularity of seizure and search of digital storage media in which relevant information and irrelevant information are intermingled, sought to firmly uphold the normative force of the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act by effectively curbing unlawful searching and collecting of irrelevant information. In light of the provisions of Article 12 of the Constitution concerning due process of law and the principle of warrant requirement, together with the fundamental purport of the various procedural provisions of the Criminal Procedure Act, including those providing for the participation of the “suspect and his or her defense counsel” in the seizure and search procedure and stating that “with respect to seized items, appropriate measures shall be taken to prevent their loss, damage, etc.” (Articles 219, 121, and 131), the Supreme Court established the doctrine that the “person subject to seizure and his or her defense counsel” may participate in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information and extended the scope of such guarantee to the “substantive person subject to seizure.”

The Supreme Court, even before the enactment of Article 243-2 of the Criminal Procedure Act, which provides for the defense counsel’s right to participate, in the suspect interrogation procedure under the former Criminal Procedure Act (the version before amendment by Act No. 8496 of June 1, 2007; hereinafter the same), where there was no express provision concerning the defense counsel’s right to participate, recognized the defense counsel’s right to participate in the suspect interrogation procedure by analogically applying the provisions of the former Criminal Procedure Act concerning the right of detention-bound defendants or suspects to meet and communicate, based on the constitutional principle of due process of law (see Supreme Court decision of November 11, 2003, 2003MO402). Recognizing the person subject to seizure’s participation right in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information and extending it to the substantive person subject to seizure is an extension of the Supreme Court’s stance to date of interpreting the Criminal Procedure Act in conformity with the Constitution so as to protect the fundamental human rights of the subject of the State’s coercive disposition from infringement.

b) The constitutional freedom of residence and the secrecy and freedom of private life are guaranteed to everyone, and the object of the warrant requirement is not limited to suspects (Constitution Articles 12, 16, and 17); therefore, the substantive person subject to seizure, as the subject to whom the participation right is attributed, which is a procedural right established to realize the constitutional due process of law and the principle of warrant requirement, is not required to be in the status of a suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. Just as in a typical seizure and search of a residence or office, the substantive owner or manager of the residence, etc. that became the object of the coercive disposition is protected by the secrecy and freedom of private life, etc., in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, the owner/manager of the digital storage medium, etc., which is the object of the coercive disposition, must receive procedural guarantees such as the participation right in accordance with the principle of warrant requirement. This is because, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium, there is no reason to endure a State agency investigating the criminal suspicion of a third party (the suspect) broadly searching, copying, and printing irrelevant information from his or her digital storage medium merely because he or she is not the suspect. Permitting this would have the same result as permitting a general warrant.

c) According to the precedents’ attitude regarding the purpose and scope of recognition of the participation right, in determining the subject to whom the participation right belongs, it is not very important who submitted the relevant digital storage medium to the law-enforcement agency or whether that person is in the status of a suspect. This is because, without needing to distinguish between the case where the manager/disposer of the electronic information directly submits the digital storage medium to the law-enforcement agency and the case where a third party such as a victim possesses or keeps it for some reason and then submits it to the law-enforcement agency, the necessity of guaranteeing participation rights to the person subject to seizure or the substantive person subject to seizure, who is the manager/disposer of the electronic information, in order to substantially protect his or her secrecy and freedom of private life and other personality-related legal interests, is the same.

The 2016DO348 en banc decision recognized the suspect’s participation right in the case where a victim or other third party unlawfully took a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect and voluntarily submitted it, because the suspect, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium and manager/disposer of the electronic information, occupies the status of the substantive object of the coercive disposition, that is, the “status of a person subject to seizure.” The manager/disposer of irrelevant information existing within the digital storage medium has an interest, as a substantive party to the seizure and search, in blocking the infringement of personality-related legal interests, etc. arising from the coercive disposition even if that person is not the suspect. Conversely, even if one is a suspect, if one is not the manager/disposer, one does not have such an interest.

The Supreme Court, only in a case where the law-enforcement agency received voluntary submission from a lodging business operator of a disguised camera, etc. secretly installed in a guest room for the purpose of illegal filming so as to photograph nudity or sexual acts, and did not afford the suspect who had secretly installed it an opportunity to participate, held that, due to the function and attributes of the relevant digital storage medium, in cases where, from the perspective of the owner’s secrecy and freedom of private life and other personality-related legal interests, there is almost no room for electronic information subject to lawful seizure through voluntary submission and electronic information not subject to it to be intermingled and, in substance, most of the electronic information stored is that which is subject to seizure, the evidence should not be denied merely because the person subject to seizure other than the possessor/custodian was not guaranteed an opportunity to participate and no inventory of seized electronic information was prepared and delivered (see the above Supreme Court decision 2019DO7342). In the case of a digital storage medium storing only relevant information, there is in substance no risk of arbitrary searching and copying of irrelevant information, so there is no concern that the purport of guaranteeing participation rights will be undermined. The above Supreme Court decision confirmed that, in such a case, even the suspect, who is the manager/disposer of the electronic information, is not a subject to whom participation rights are guaranteed, thereby showing that the basis of the attribution of participation rights lies not in the status of suspect but in the status of being subject to the coercive disposition such as seizure and search and thereby suffering substantial infringement of secrecy of private life and other personality-related legal interests.

d) In this way, in our criminal justice system and investigative practice, the person subject to seizure’s participation right guaranteed in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information has become a practical yet essential procedural right and institution that can constitutionally control the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency. By granting the person subjected to coercive disposition the opportunity to directly confirm on site the manner in which the seizure is executed and to raise objections, it is possible to effectively deter the searching and collecting of irrelevant information contrary to the warrant requirement. For the participation right to function substantially in accordance with its purpose, it is necessary to grant the participation right to the subject to whom the legal interests, such as secrecy and freedom of private life, that may be infringed by the search, copying, and printing of irrelevant information belong.

e) The majority opinion, based on the fact that the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein are evidence concerning Non-Indicted Person 3’s suspicion of concealment of evidence, held that Non-Indicted Person 3 corresponds to a “person with a substantive interest” in the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information stored therein and has an “interest in participation” throughout the search, copying, and printing process, and that, since participation rights were guaranteed to Non-Indicted Person 3, the seizure and search procedure was lawful even though the owner Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. did not participate, finding the basis for the guarantee of participation rights in “substantive interest concerning the electronic information” or “interest in participation” in relation to the suspect status or the coercive disposition against evidence “related” to the criminal facts. However, this runs counter to the precedents concerning the basis for and object of the guarantee of participation rights and is improper. As examined above, the precedents declared the guarantee of participation rights in order to limit the object of seizure to electronic information concerning the facts suspected of crime and to prevent arbitrary copying, etc. of electronic information that is “unrelated” thereto; accordingly, the interest in participation under the precedents lies in the protection of interests concerning “irrelevant evidence.” The above Supreme Court decision 2019DO7342 also did not regard only having an interest in electronic information “related to the facts charged,” i.e. relevant information, as an “interest in participation.”

The majority opinion, while emphasizing the importance of the electronic information stored in a digital storage medium in modern society and the protection of secrecy and freedom of private life, the right to informational self-determination, etc. along with the due process of law and the principle of warrant requirement that the Constitution and the Criminal Procedure Act seek to realize, adopts the contradictory stance of interpreting very narrowly the meaning of the “substantive person subject to seizure,” who is the subject guaranteed the participation right, centering on the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. Thereby, the majority opinion has substantially nullified the achievements made by the precedents so far in responding to the constitutional demand that due process of law and the principle of warrant requirement be realized by declaring the participation-right doctrine in the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning electronic information and expanding the scope of the subjects to whom it belongs. As a result, in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, the door to the procedural right called the participation right, which the Supreme Court opened for the guarantee of fundamental rights of the person subject to seizure or the substantive person subject to seizure, has been half-closed again. It is no appropriate measure to realize the principle of relevance in the seizure and search of a digital storage medium to say that it is sufficient to guarantee participation rights only to the suspect, who is the direct and formal party to the coercive disposition, even though that person has no special interest in preventing arbitrary searching of irrelevant information, and that there is no need to guarantee participation rights even to the owner/manager of the digital storage medium; this is tantamount to abandoning the protection of due process of law and the principle of warrant requirement against infringement of personality-related legal interests concerning irrelevant information that may arise for the owner/manager of the digital storage medium.

2) Guarantee of participation rights where the formal person subject to seizure and the substantive person subject to seizure are separate

Where, in addition to the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium, who is the direct object of the law-enforcement agency’s coercive disposition and the formal person subject to seizure, the owner/manager exists separately, it is necessary to regard the latter as the substantive person subject to seizure and guarantee participation rights to him or her as well.

a) With the development of technology, as the portability and mobility of digital storage media increased, it has become common for an owner/manager to exist separately from the actual possessor and custodian of the digital storage medium. First, there are cases where the digital storage medium leaves the owner/manager’s possession and comes to be in the possession or custody of a third party regardless of the owner/manager’s will. This includes cases where the owner/manager loses the digital storage medium, or where it becomes the object of a criminal act such as theft or embezzlement of lost property, or where a third party takes the digital storage medium arbitrarily without the consent of the owner/manager. On the other hand, there are also cases where the digital storage medium comes to be in the possession or custody of a third party based on a possessory-mediated relationship formed according to the owner/manager’s will. This would include cases where the owner/manager requests a specialist repair shop to repair the digital storage medium or deposits it with a bank’s safe deposit box, cases where a child temporarily borrows and uses a parent’s mobile phone, or cases where the owner/manager entrusts his or her digital storage medium to a family member or acquaintance living separately for safekeeping. A case where the principal offender, intending to conceal evidence concerning the suspected facts, hands over a digital storage medium that he or she owned and controlled to an evidence concealer may also fall under the latter category in that it is based on a possessory-mediated relationship formed according to the owner/manager principal offender’s will.

b) The 2016DO348 en banc decision recognized the suspect’s participation right in the former situation, where a victim or other third party took, without the suspect’s knowledge, a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect from the crime scene and voluntarily submitted it to the law-enforcement agency, that is, the case in which the digital storage medium left the owner/manager’s possession regardless of his or her will. This doctrine must likewise apply to the latter situation, where a third party possessed or kept the digital storage medium on the basis of a possessory-mediated relationship formed according to the owner/manager’s will and coercive disposition is made against the third party. When determining whether the subject falls within the object of the participation-right guarantee, there is no reason to treat differently the case where the separation of the owner/manager and actual possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium occurred according to the owner/manager’s will and the case where it did not. In both cases, they are the same in that the manager/disposer of the electronic information is the subject to whom personality-related legal interests, which may be infringed by the law-enforcement agency’s arbitrary copying of irrelevant information, etc., belong.

3) Criteria for determining the substantive person subject to seizure

a) Whether one corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure as the subject to whom the participation right belongs must be determined on the basis of the factual state outwardly and objectively recognizable at the time of seizure and search, such as who actually dominated and managed the relevant digital storage medium until the time of seizure and search or a temporally close point thereto, and whether, based on the objective circumstances surrounding the progress of the investigation and the loss of possession or possessory mediation concerning the digital storage medium, the law-enforcement agency could recognize that an owner/manager existed separately from the possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium. Internal, subjective circumstances between related persons that the law-enforcement agency could not recognize at the time of seizure and search, or a legal and retrospective judgment concerning the attribution of rights under civil law, are not to be considered. In addition, even a person who actually dominated and managed the digital storage medium is excluded from the subject to whom the participation right belongs if he or she transferred it to a third party according to his or her own will or abandoned the right of domination and control over it (see the above Supreme Court decision 2021DO11170).

b) When, as above, the substantive person subject to seizure is determined based on the objectively and outwardly recognizable factual state at the time of seizure and search, there is little risk of causing confusion and side effects in investigative practice, such as being unable to identify the person with the participation right or unreasonably expanding the scope of the guarantee of participation rights to many persons. This is because, unless there are special circumstances suggesting the existence of a separate manager/disposer, it is acceptable to regard the actual possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium at the time of seizure and search as the manager/disposer of the electronic information, and it is sufficient to regard a person as the substantive person subject to seizure only when there are special circumstances from which the law-enforcement agency can, based on the objectively and outwardly recognizable factual state, acknowledge that a person who exclusively holds authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information exists separately from the actual possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium. For example, this includes cases where, from an objective and outward perspective, a customer’s digital storage medium kept in a bank safe deposit box or a client’s computer temporarily kept by a computer repair company that has been entrusted with repair is plainly separated, by its very nature, from the actual possessor/custodian and the exclusive manager/disposer of the electronic information, or where the law-enforcement agency can recognize, through the statement of the actual possessor/custodian of the digital storage medium or the progress of the investigation, that a separate exclusive manager/disposer of the electronic information exists.

c) The majority opinion stated that, in light of the circumstances surrounding the concealment and voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, the person who actually possessed the instant hard disk drive at the time of seizure and search or at a time close thereto was Non-Indicted Person 3, and thus, absent other special circumstances, the person in a position to de facto retain and exercise the authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information stored in the instant hard disk drive was also Non-Indicted Person 3; however, this is not proper. In this case, in light of the progress of the respective investigative procedures concerning Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., the principal offenders, and Non-Indicted Person 3, the evidence concealer, as well as the content of the statements made by Non-Indicted Person 3 to the prosecutor at the time he voluntarily submitted the instant hard disk drive, and other factual circumstances objectively and outwardly recognizable to the law-enforcement agency, the law-enforcement agency could recognize, at the time it accepted the voluntary submission, that, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3, who was the actual possessor/custodian of the instant hard disk drive, there existed Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., who were the exclusive managers/disposers of the electronic information. In particular, the fact that the law-enforcement agency, while investigating the suspect facts against the principal offender, took as a suspect for the offense of concealment of evidence the person who was concealing the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender and accepted the concealed item by voluntary submission, by itself means that, at the time of voluntary submission, the law-enforcement agency was aware of the existence of the principal offender, who is an element of the offense of concealment of evidence, and that the concealed item belonged to or was under the control of the principal offender.

d. Scope of the guarantee of participation rights in the case of the principal offender and the evidence concealer

1) The legal doctrine of guaranteeing participation rights should likewise apply to cases where the principal offender instructs the concealment of evidence by handing over to the evidence concealer a digital storage medium in which electronic information constituting evidence concerning the suspected facts is stored, and the evidence concealer keeps and conceals it and then submits it to the law-enforcement agency in the form of seizure or voluntary submission. In such a case, the principal offender, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium that is in a typical possessory-mediated relationship vis-à-vis the evidence concealer, who is the actual possessor/custodian of the concealed item, corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure, who has an interest in protecting rights such as the secrecy and freedom of private life by preventing the searching and collecting of irrelevant information in the course of seizure and search. Even if the evidence concealer voluntarily submitted it to the law-enforcement agency in the status of a suspect for concealment of evidence, the substantive person subject to seizure is the principal offender, and participation rights should also be guaranteed to him or her. Because the evidence concealer, who is not the subject to whom the personality-related legal interests concerning irrelevant information within the concealed digital storage medium belong, has no incentive to actually exercise participation rights even if such rights are guaranteed, the purpose of guaranteeing participation rights for the sake of the principle of warrant requirement cannot be realized merely by excluding the principal offender and guaranteeing participation rights only to the evidence concealer. Nor can it be prevented, in the seizure and search procedure of the concealed digital storage medium, that irrelevant information concerning the principal offender’s private life is broadly and indiscriminately collected by the law-enforcement agency. In this case as well, Non-Indicted Person 3, the evidence concealer, waived the exercise of his participation right.

2) Where the principal offender, by handing over to the evidence concealer a digital storage medium in which electronic information constituting evidence concerning his or her own suspected facts is stored, instructed concealment, unless there are other special circumstances that would justify recognizing that he or she definitively and completely abandoned the authority to manage and dispose of that electronic information, it cannot be concluded solely from the fact that actual and direct possession of the digital storage medium was transferred to the evidence concealer by such handover that the principal offender transferred or abandoned the authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information or that the interest in the participation right, which enables protection of personality-related legal interests such as the secrecy and freedom of private life by excluding the law-enforcement agency’s search of irrelevant information intermingled in the digital storage medium, has disappeared.

Considering the characteristics of digital storage media and electronic information, the purpose of their concealment, the circumstances of the concealment of evidence, whether the concealed evidence is to be returned, and the true intentions of the parties, it is natural and consistent with experience rules to interpret that the principal offender merely entrusted the storage to the evidence concealer on a temporary basis through concealment of the digital storage medium until the risk of exposure or discovery of relevant information disappeared, and that, once that risk disappeared, the principal offender intended to regain actual dominion over the digital storage medium, including the electronic information that is irrelevant evidence. Owing to the characteristics of the possessory-mediated relationship formed between the principal offender and the evidence concealer concerning the concealment of a digital storage medium in which relevant information and irrelevant information are intermingled, the principal offender should be understood as having concealed the digital storage medium with the intention not only of evading his or her criminal responsibility but also of preserving and keeping the irrelevant information, which has personal and personality-related value, and of receiving it back at an appropriate time in the future, in a situation where it is technically difficult to sift out and discard or destroy only the relevant information inside the digital storage medium.

3) The majority opinion viewed that Non-Indicted Person 1, the principal offender, expressed an intention to waive or wholly transfer the exclusive right of domination and control over the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 until the indefinite time of “completion of the investigation,” by handing over the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3, requesting that it be hidden “until the investigation into himself is over,” with the purpose of concealing the very existence of the instant hard disk drive, which is evidence concerning the principal-offense suspicion, and thereby under the purpose of concealing and severing the outward connection between himself and the instant hard disk drive, etc.

However, the majority opinion exceeds the bounds of reasonable interpretation of intent in the structure of the “principal offender and evidence concealer,” which is a typical possessory-mediated relationship, and is not proper.

In addition, the majority opinion errs in equating this with cases where one instructs concealment of tangible objects that are themselves evidence concerning the suspected crime, such as a weapon used in a murder offense, narcotics or syringes provided for a drug-related offense, etc., overlooking the specificity and importance of the intermingling of irrelevant evidence in a digital storage medium with respect to the guarantee of participation rights. If the context of the meaning of personality-related legal interests in the coercive disposition such as seizure and search of a digital storage medium intermingled with relevant evidence and irrelevant evidence had originally been the same as in the case of the above weapon, narcotics, or other evidence objects, there would have been no need for the precedents to establish the doctrine of guaranteeing participation rights to the person subject to seizure in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information.

The majority opinion is also confusing the issue of interpreting intent concerning the domination and control over the electronic information that is the concealed item between the principal offender and the evidence concealer in this case, or the issue of identifying the subject to whom the participation right belongs, with the assessment of illegality, culpability, or the existence of criminal responsibility for the act of Non-Indicted Person 1 in infringing the judicial function concerning the investigation of the principal offense through instigation of concealment of evidence. If there were no act of instigation of concealment of evidence by the principal offender, that is, if the principal offender had concealed the digital storage medium by handing it over to a third party unaware of the concealment intent while concealing such intent, would the majority opinion really take the same view and exclude the principal offender’s participation right? If the conclusion regarding the existence or nonexistence of the principal offender’s participation right differs in the two cases, this can only be seen as confusing the assessment of the punishability of the instigation of concealment and the issue of identifying the subject to whom participation rights belong.

4) In this case, the majority opinion, where the law-enforcement agency, while investigating the principal-offense facts against the principal offender, voluntarily received from the evidence concealer the digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the principal offender that he or she had concealed, overlooked the fact that the investigative procedure against the evidence concealer is, in substance, conducted as part of the investigative procedure against the principal offender, and, without exploring the legal issue of who is the substantive person subject to seizure as the subject to whom participation rights belong in the possessory-mediated relationship of the “principal offender and evidence concealer” structure, handled the matter as an issue of interpreting whether the principal offender had transferred or abandoned the authority to manage and dispose of the digital storage medium to the evidence concealer. That is not the proper attitude a Supreme Court, a bulwark for the protection of human rights, should take.

e. Determination concerning this case

1) Based on the following circumstances, judged from the factual state outwardly and objectively recognizable at the time of seizure and search pursuant to the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, it is difficult to see that, until the time of Non-Indicted Person 3’s voluntary submission and at a temporally close point thereto, Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., who were the principal offenders, actually dominated and managed the instant hard disk drive on the basis of actual possession or of a possessory-mediated relationship through Non-Indicted Person 3, while retaining and exercising exclusive authority to manage and dispose of the electronic information stored therein as the subject to whom legal interests belong, and that they had lost neither the authority to manage and dispose of it nor ownership or control. Accordingly, it is proper to regard Non-Indicted Person 1, etc. as the substantive persons subject to seizure with respect to that electronic information.

a) The instant hard disk drive was installed in the personal computers placed in the studies, etc. within the residence of Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. Even if one examines the progress of the offense of concealment of evidence by Non-Indicted Person 3 and Non-Indicted Person 1 that arose during the investigation of the principal-offense facts against Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., as well as the content of the electronic information stored in the instant hard disk drive, it can be said that Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. were exclusively using the instant hard disk drive until August 31, 2019, only 11 days before Non-Indicted Person 3’s voluntary submission.

b) The instant hard disk drive is the digital storage medium of a computer that Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. had personally used for a long period at their residence, and it stores not only evidence related to the principal-offense facts against Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. but also various personal information of Non-Indicted Person 1 and members of his family. In light of the subjective value of the instant hard disk drive as personal information, it appears that Non-Indicted Person 1 handed the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 with the intention that it be hidden in preparation for future prosecution investigations, not to eliminate it. Until just before voluntarily submitting the instant hard disk drive to the law-enforcement agency, Non-Indicted Person 3 was keeping and managing it in a personal locker, etc. at the gym in accordance with Non-Indicted Person 1’s instruction to hide it, and he also returned a separate personal computer in the professor’s office at (Name 4 omitted) University, which he had concealed together with the instant hard disk drive, upon Non-Indicted Person 1’s request. Under such a special form of possessory-mediated relationship formed by receiving the instant hard disk drive, Non-Indicted Person 3 concealed it while intending, whenever instructed by Non-Indicted Person 1, to return it to Non-Indicted Person 1, etc. and proceed to dispose of it in accordance with the purpose of the instruction. Thus, it is difficult to say that, at the time of the voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive, Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. had completely lost the authority to manage and dispose of, or ownership/control over, the instant hard disk drive.

c) In light of the investigative progress around that time and the prosecutor’s statements at the time of Non-Indicted Person 3’s voluntary submission, it can be said that the law-enforcement agency also knew, or could sufficiently know, the ownership/control status of the instant hard disk drive and who the exclusive user was when it accepted the instant hard disk drive by voluntary submission.

2) In the series of processes such as searching and extracting the electronic information stored therein after seizing the instant hard disk drive by voluntary submission from Non-Indicted Person 3 during the investigation of the principal-offense facts against Non-Indicted Person 1, the law-enforcement agency must guarantee an opportunity to participate to Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., who are the substantive persons subject to seizure of the instant hard disk drive and the electronic information, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3, who is the person subject to seizure. However, in such a series of processes, the law-enforcement agency did not guarantee participation rights to Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., who are the substantive persons subject to seizure, in addition to Non-Indicted Person 3, who is the person subject to seizure.

Accordingly, the electronic information in the instant hard disk drive seized by the law-enforcement agency constitutes illegally obtained evidence and cannot be used as evidence of guilt. It is also difficult to find any special circumstances to recognize an exception thereto. The statements of the related persons collected by the law-enforcement agency on the basis of that illegally obtained evidence also constitute derivative evidence based on illegally obtained evidence and likewise cannot be used as evidence to establish guilt.

3) In this case, there is room to view that, excluding evidence without admissibility, it is difficult to say that the remaining evidence alone proved the facts charged in this case beyond a reasonable doubt. Nevertheless, the lower court maintained the first-instance judgment, which found the facts charged in this case guilty for the reasons stated in the opinion. Such a determination by the lower court contains errors affecting the judgment by misapprehending the legal principles concerning participation rights in the seizure of items voluntarily submitted and the exclusionary rule for illegally obtained evidence, and by failing to conduct the necessary examination.

For the foregoing reasons, I state that I cannot agree with the majority opinion.

5. Concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion

With respect to the subject of participation rights for securing procedural legality in the seizure and search process of electronic information, in light of the holdings and purport of a series of precedents that guaranteed participation rights to the suspect when the suspect, rather than the formal person subject to seizure, corresponds to the “substantive person subject to seizure,” the scope of seizure and search resulting from Non-Indicted Person 3’s voluntary submission of the instant hard disk drive is limited to evidence related to the criminal facts that motivated it, namely “the crime of concealment of evidence.” Therefore, procedural legality is clearly established by guaranteeing participation rights to Non-Indicted Person 3, who is both the suspect in the relevant criminal facts and the actual dominator and manager of the digital storage medium that is the relevant evidence, and it does not appear necessary to provide further argumentation in this regard. Below, we supplement the grounds of the majority opinion only to the extent necessary to prevent misunderstanding of the majority opinion’s purport among the matters pointed out in the dissenting opinion.

a. The purport of the precedents concerning participation rights

The “substantive person subject to seizure” concept in the precedents is a kind of instrumental concept devised to overcome the gap between statutory wording and the basic ideas centered on the constitutional principle of due process and warrant requirement in the phase of guaranteeing participation rights concerning seizure and search of electronic information, which traditional seizure and search doctrine premised on tangible objects did not anticipate. The purport contained in the series of precedents concerning participation rights is that, in seizure and search of a digital storage medium in which it is difficult to know the subject to whom a multitude and wide variety of individual pieces of stored information belong, the matter should in principle be regulated centering on the person subject to seizure, who is the manager/disposer of all electronic information, but where the person subject to seizure has no substantive interest whatsoever in the criminal facts suspected and the seized items, there is no reason to participate in the seizure and search procedure; on the other hand, in order to prevent the possibility that indiscriminate seizure and search execution may occur without anyone’s participation by excluding a suspect who has a substantive interest on the ground that he or she is not the person subject to seizure, the problem is resolved through the concept of the “substantive person subject to seizure.”

In light of this stance of the precedents, where the evidence concealer voluntarily submits, with respect to the criminal facts of concealment of evidence, the digital storage medium that is the object of concealment, even if the digital storage medium belongs to the principal offender, it is sufficient to grant participation rights to the evidence concealer, who is the suspect in and the cause of the voluntary submission seizure and search, and who also corresponds to the person subject to seizure, and there is no need further to regard the principal offender as the substantive person subject to seizure and recognize participation rights for him or her as well. In this case, because the suspect, who is the evidence concealer, voluntarily submits a digital storage medium in his or her possession or custody that is recognized as related to the investigation into his or her own criminal facts, the evidence concealer has direct, substantive, and legal interests as both suspect and person subject to seizure in the seizure and search flowing therefrom. The 2016DO348 en banc decision, in recognizing participation rights for a suspect who is not the formal person subject to seizure as the “substantive person subject to seizure,” addressed a different plane of discussion from the evidence concealer’s voluntary submission case, because in that case the person subject to seizure, who was the formal voluntary submitter, was merely a victim of the criminal facts and the purpose of guaranteeing the opportunity to participate to that person alone could not substantially realize the purpose of the participation-right guarantee.

In short, where the suspect in the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search not only is related to the facts suspected but also has direct, substantive, and legal interests by dominating and managing the digital storage medium and electronic evidence that are the objects of the seizure and search, if participation rights are guaranteed to that suspect, who simultaneously occupies the status of interested person and person subject to seizure, the procedural legality concerning the participation right can be viewed as thereby satisfied and completed. Unless there are other special circumstances, there is no need to separately posit the substantive person subject to seizure in such a case.

Turning to this case, the instant hard disk drive was voluntarily submitted to the law-enforcement agency by Non-Indicted Person 3, the evidence concealer, while he was dominating and managing it after receiving it from Non-Indicted Person 1, and, in relation to the concealment of evidence that constituted his own criminal facts, Non-Indicted Person 3 has direct, substantive, and legal interests in the instant hard disk drive, which is the evidence. Accordingly, insofar as the seizure and search procedure for the instant hard disk drive was conducted with the participation of Non-Indicted Person 3, who is the rightful interested party, the procedural legality of that procedure is, in principle, satisfied by affording Non-Indicted Person 3 the opportunity to participate. Further, the dissenting opinion, which would allow an anti-constitutional result infringing the legal interests concerning secrecy and freedom of private life, etc. by not even granting participation rights to Non-Indicted Person 1, etc., who handed over the instant hard disk drive for the purpose of destroying evidence, is difficult to accept.

b. Recognition of participation rights based on the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search

Recognition of the participation right, including the concept of the “substantive person subject to seizure,” should in principle be based on the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. The scope and limits of guaranteeing participation rights should be determined through a balancing of the purpose sought to be achieved through the procedure and the interests infringed thereby, taking into account the characteristics of the investigative procedure. This is because the purport of the participation right is to minimize infringement of the legal interests of the person subject to seizure in the course of a real property-based coercive disposition, while at the same time the ideal of criminal justice—discovering the substantive truth through prompt and effective investigation—must also be harmoniously realized to the extent that such legal interests are not essentially infringed.

The dissenting opinion’s purport is that participation rights in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information should be understood separately from the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search. However, criminal facts are both the ultimate object and purpose to be elucidated through coercive investigation and the basis and cause of the issuance of a warrant and the seizure and search, and the electronic information that is searched, copied, and printed in the process of executing the warrant is also the direct object related to the relevant facts. Therefore, the criminal facts concerned are the most important consideration in the process of searching, copying, and printing relevant electronic information, and it is neither natural nor in accord with the purport of participation rights to disregard precisely the most important element in the relevant criminal procedure when recognizing that procedural right. The precedents concerning this have attempted to rationally interpret, in light of actual and concrete circumstances, the provisions on seizure and search centered on tangible objects, which do not adequately reflect the characteristics of electronic information and its storage medium; however, the dissenting opinion overemphasizes certain phrases from the precedents or understands them superficially, and in the end develops an argument that does not fit the wording of the Criminal Procedure Act and is also detached from the ideal of criminal justice, so it is difficult to accept. This is because the question of whether seizure and search of electronic information related to criminal facts and the guarantee of participation rights are centered on the digital storage medium and its manager/controller, versus the question of whether they are understood separately from the criminal facts, are entirely different matters.

Furthermore, understanding participation rights on the premise of the criminal facts is also consistent with the warrant-execution practice, where promptness, expedition, timeliness, and secrecy are important, because it enables concise and clear identification of the subject of the participation right. The above Supreme Court decision 2021DO11170, premised on the 2016DO348 en banc decision that where a third party voluntarily submitted a suspect’s digital storage medium in relation to the suspect’s criminal facts, participation rights should be guaranteed to the suspect, who is the substantive person subject to seizure, held that whether the digital storage medium falls within the category for which participation rights are recognized for the suspect should be determined based on the objectively and outwardly recognizable factual state. This is also to harmoniously realize the ideals of criminal justice—protection of fundamental rights and discovery of substantive truth—by reasonably setting the scope of participation rights in light of the on-site nature of seizure and search, etc. The dissenting opinion’s approach, which determines participation rights solely on the basis of the possibility of infringement of legal interests concerning irrelevant information in the process of searching, copying, and printing electronic information, ignores the essence of participation rights derived from coercive investigation procedures concerning the facts charged and presupposes that the law-enforcement agency’s seizure and search is, as a rule or in general, exploratory and searching and thus unlawful. Although the concern it raises is understandable, this is a matter to be resolved through the rational interpretation of the relevant legal doctrines, including the participation right, as well as through the application of strict rules of evidence; it is not possible, on that basis, to construct a general doctrine premised on such an exceptional situation.

c. Transfer of the authority to manage and dispose and the existence of the participation right

Where a third party voluntarily submits a digital storage medium belonging to or under the control of the suspect, in order for the suspect to be evaluated as the substantive party to the seizure and search of all electronic information stored in that digital storage medium and to receive participation rights, the suspect must, until the time of seizure and search or a temporally close point thereto, have actually dominated and managed the relevant digital storage medium while retaining and exercising the “exclusive” authority to manage and dispose of all electronic information in that digital storage medium, and must not otherwise have transferred or abandoned it to a third party according to his or her will. Meanwhile, as precedent has clearly stated, “authority to manage and dispose” here is for the purpose of setting a reasonable scope of protection for participation rights by harmonizing protection of fundamental rights and the ideal of discovery of substantive truth in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, and is not for the purpose of determining private-law rights and relationships from a legal and retrospective perspective according to the attribution of rights under civil law (the above Supreme Court decision 2021DO11170).

In light of such legal principles, the reason Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. are not regarded as the substantive persons subject to seizure and thus participation rights are not recognized in the process of voluntary submission and seizure of the instant hard disk drive and the stored electronic information is self-evident. Since Non-Indicted Person 1 handed the instant hard disk drive to Non-Indicted Person 3 and instructed concealment of evidence, and Non-Indicted Person 3 concealed it, it is clear that Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc. thereby lost actual domination and management of the instant hard disk drive; furthermore, the authority to manage and dispose of all stored electronic information was transferred to Non-Indicted Person 3, and in fact Non-Indicted Person 3, by concealing the instant hard disk drive in a place known only to him, even placed the entire digital storage medium and built-in electronic information in a situation where he could, according to his own judgment, manage and dispose of them at will so that they would not be exposed to the law-enforcement agency. Accordingly, at least for Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc., it must be regarded that they had already reached a state where they could no longer retain and exercise the “exclusive” authority to manage and dispose.

Moreover, the fact that the principal offender not only conceals the evidence himself or herself but also instructs the evidence concealer, who is the principal offender in form, and thereby causes the state of concealment of evidence, exceeds the scope of legitimate defense rights. Even in light of the fact that the principal offender intentionally created a state in which evidence had departed from its position while infringing the judicial function of the State, it is normatively consistent to regard that the participation right, which is a procedural right in criminal proceedings, or the authority to manage and dispose underlying it, is no longer reserved to the principal offender as a result of such infringement of the State’s judicial function. This also accords with the ideal of criminal justice, which seeks to harmonize discovery of the substantive truth and the principle of due process and thereby realize justice. As noted above, with respect to the criminal facts that caused the voluntary submission in this case or the instant hard disk drive, which is the evidence in question, Non-Indicted Person 3 corresponds to a person having direct, substantive, and legal interests; therefore, by guaranteeing Non-Indicted Person 3 the opportunity to participate in the seizure and search process concerning the instant hard disk drive, the procedural legality thereof can, in principle, be recognized, and this is all the more so because there are no special circumstances that would otherwise require viewing that multiple separate participation-right holders exist.

This is not an evaluation of the illegality of Non-Indicted Person 1’s act of instigating concealment of evidence, but rather an evaluation grounded in the purport of precedent following the loss of Non-Indicted Persons 1, etc.’s “exclusive” authority to manage and dispose of the instant hard disk drive, so the dissenting opinion’s criticism on this point is incorrect. The dissenting opinion’s argument that a different conclusion can be reached on the basis of civil-law doctrines such as possessory-mediated relationships is likewise difficult to accept for the same reason, even without resort to the same civil-law doctrines of anti-social conduct or performance for unlawful cause, etc.

d. Other circumstances

The other grounds advanced by the dissenting opinion likewise cannot be adopted as general legal doctrine or as the conclusion of this case and the subsumption doctrine of precedent.

One point to add in this regard is that the majority opinion does not differ from the dissenting opinion even as to the direction of guaranteeing participation rights in seizure and search procedures proposed by the dissenting opinion. Compared with the legislative examples or trial practice of major foreign jurisdictions, our doctrine concerning participation rights in seizure and search procedures is still in the process of formation. Its orientation lies in realizing, in the seizure and search of electronic information, the constitutional principles of warrant requirement and due process while preventing infringement of fundamental rights such as the secrecy and freedom of private life and the right to informational self-determination, but the essence of coercive investigation procedures is, in any event, to function so as to secure procedural legality and legitimacy in the seizure and search process concerning specific criminal facts suspected. In addition, since it must not be substantially detached from the ideal of criminal justice—discovering the substantive truth through prompt and effective investigation—it is necessary to approach carefully so as not to lose direction, but while striking a balance among conflicting values, also not to deviate from concrete propriety and common-sense conclusions. In that respect, I would like to make clear that, at least in this case, it is only that the dissenting opinion cannot be adopted; the majority opinion does not negate all of the arguments or purport developed by the dissenting opinion.

6. Concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justice Oh Kyung-mi on the dissenting opinion

The situation in which the smartphone you lost recently by leaving it in a taxi is illegally distributed and used in a voice phishing crime and then seized by the law-enforcement agency can happen at any time. The same is true of the situation where your child, who had briefly borrowed and used your smartphone, is caught engaging in illegal filming on the subway and voluntarily submits it to the law-enforcement agency. If the law-enforcement agency learns that you are the owner/manager of the smartphone and that your personal information is stored in it, is the procedural legality concerning participation rights satisfied and completed by recognizing participation rights only for the voice-phishing offender or your child, who are the persons subject to seizure and suspects with “direct, substantive, and legal interests” based on the criminal facts in the course of the search and extraction process? The concurring opinion of Supreme Court Justices Ahn Cheol-sang, Noh Tae-ak, and Cheon Dae-yeop on the majority opinion (hereinafter referred to as the “majority concurring opinion”) answers yes. In such a situation, can one accept that the law-enforcement agency searches and extracts your personal information from your smartphone without your knowledge? Was the participation right in the seizure and search of electronic information recognized by precedent such a flimsy and formal right? The dissenting opinion says no. That is precisely the issue in this case.

a. Concerning the assertion that participation rights must be recognized based on the criminal facts

1) The majority concurring opinion’s assertion that the subject of participation rights must be recognized centering on the criminal facts amounts, in the end, to recognizing participation rights based on “suspect status.” Such an assertion not only contravenes the explicit stance and flow of the precedents concerning the purport of guaranteeing participation rights, but also contradicts the majority concurring opinion’s own reasoning.

The precedents have repeatedly and explicitly stated that the practical significance and purport of participation rights lie in protecting the person subject to seizure, who is placed at risk of indiscriminate searching and collecting of information unrelated to the suspect facts that caused the seizure and search, in the opportunity for lawful coercive disposition concerning relevant information. The need to be protected from such risks is unrelated to whether the person subject to seizure is a suspect. Rather, from the standpoint of balancing interests, a person subject to seizure who is not a suspect would likely find it even more difficult to accept having to endure disclosure of private life for the investigation of another person (the suspect) unrelated to himself or herself. The above Supreme Court decision 2019DO7342 clearly stated that, even where a suspect who had secretly installed a disguised camera, etc. in a lodging establishment solely for the purpose of illegal filming corresponds to the substantive person subject to seizure as the manager/disposer of the electronic information, there is no need to recognize participation rights, thereby making clear that if there is no risk of infringement of the person subject to seizure’s legal interests concerning irrelevant information, there is no practical benefit in guaranteeing participation rights. By contrast, the majority concurring opinion’s argument that participation rights should be attributed centering on the criminal facts or suspect status can, in effect, be seen as conflicting with the above precedents’ legal doctrine.

Moreover, the majority concurring opinion also stated that the purport of the precedents concerning participation rights is to regulate, in principle, seizure and search of a digital storage medium centering on the person subject to seizure, who is the manager/disposer of all electronic information, but to use the concept of the substantive person subject to seizure instrumentally in order to solve the problem of no participation-right holder where the person subject to seizure has no substantive interest in the criminal facts and the seized items. Even so, the majority concurring opinion’s argument that the subject of participation rights should be recognized centering on the criminal facts lacks consistency.

2) The majority concurring opinion uses “direct, substantive, and legal interest” in the criminal facts or seized items as an important indicator for recognizing participation rights, but such an interest is unrelated to the purport of the precedents in which participation rights were recognized or to their protected sphere, so it is not logical to use it as an indicator for the attribution of participation rights.

Although the exact purport of “direct, substantive, and legal interest in the criminal facts or seized items” as used by the majority concurring opinion is not clear, it appears roughly to mean “the interest of a suspect, from the suspect’s standpoint, in avoiding exposure of evidence concerning his or her own criminal facts to the law-enforcement agency in order to evade criminal liability,” that is, the “suspect’s defense-right-related interest concerning relevant evidence.” If so, this is not directly related to the purport of participation-right guarantees explicitly declared by the precedents. What exists to protect such an interest is the traditionally recognized principle of due process and the principle of warrant requirement itself. It is precisely that, unless there is a warrant lawfully issued by a judge through the specification and substantiation of the suspect’s criminal suspicion, the “suspect’s defense-right-related interest concerning relevant evidence” is not infringed. Once a warrant has been lawfully issued, both the suspect and any third party must endure the coercive disposition of relevant evidence, which is evidence within the line drawn by the warrant, i.e. within the “principle of relevance.” This is the active aspect of the warrant requirement vis-à-vis the law-enforcement agency. In this area, participation rights do not have special significance.

Participation rights function in the passive aspect of the warrant requirement vis-à-vis the law-enforcement agency. That is, they are the power to restrain and deny effect when the law-enforcement agency’s coercive disposition extends to irrelevant evidence, i.e. evidence outside the line drawn by the warrant, the “principle of relevance.” Participation rights protect, in this area, the interests of the subject of the coercive disposition in respect of irrelevant evidence outside the above line.
