In the end, the “direct, substantive, and legal interest” referred to by the majority concurring opinion is not much different from the “relevance” that determines the scope of the warrant’s effect, and, at least as to recognition of participation rights, it has no meaning beyond being the benchmark for distinguishing relevant evidence from irrelevant evidence. The sphere protected by participation rights according to precedent is the sphere of irrelevant evidence, and it does not overlap at all with the sphere in which a “direct, substantive, and legal interest in the criminal facts or seized items” is recognized.

b. Concerning the criticism of “detachment from the criminal facts”

The majority concurring opinion points out that the dissenting opinion understood participation rights separately from the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search, but this is a misunderstanding of the dissenting opinion and is an assertion that cannot logically stand. Participation rights form one pillar of the warrant requirement and, by their nature, cannot be discussed detached from the criminal facts.

Even under the dissenting opinion, the criminal facts substantially affect the setting of the scope or limits of participation rights. In order to set the scope of the guarantee of participation rights, a distinction between relevant information and irrelevant information must first be made, and this is based on the criminal facts. In other words, the line of the “principle of relevance,” which functions in the passive aspect of the warrant requirement vis-à-vis the law-enforcement agency, is set based on the criminal facts. The area outside that line is the area of participation rights. In the end, the concept of the substantive person subject to seizure according to the dissenting opinion is by no means understood detached from the criminal facts that caused the seizure and search; rather, it is a concept associated with irrelevant evidence premised on the criminal facts.

c. Implications for investigative practice for protecting fundamental rights suited to a highly advanced information society

A smartphone spends all day with its owner/manager in daily life and stores his or her personal information in detail. Corporations cannot conduct business activities without large-capacity computers, servers, and the exchange and storage of information through the internet. Furthermore, due to the increase in portability and mobility, it often happens that digital storage media leave the possession of the owner/manager, either according to his or her will or regardless of it, and come to be in the possession or custody of another person. In the seizure and search process of the law-enforcement agency, one frequently encounters situations in which a suspect conceals or discards his or her mobile phone or computer, etc. The dissenting opinion assumes a relation of dispossession or a possessory-mediated relationship, etc., as the situation in which participation-right issues arise. It is not unusual for the owner/manager of a digital storage medium and the law-enforcement agency to stand in opposition within such a relationship.

With the dramatic development of information technology, the problematic situations surrounding digital storage media will become even more complex in the future, and the proposition that the coercive disposition of the law-enforcement agency concerning such matters must be constitutionally controlled so that investigative practice develops in a direction that guarantees fundamental rights has become self-evident. The Supreme Court should present, as a guarantee of the procedural right demanded by such a proposition, the standards for seizure and search procedures of electronic information that can both respond to the constitutional demand by guaranteeing procedural rights and satisfy the ideals of criminal justice through discovery of the substantive truth. The dissenting opinion, reflecting the factors considered by precedent in developing the participation-right doctrine, typifies situations of seizure and search of electronic information and establishes a unified standard capable of protecting the interests of the substantive person subject to seizure based on the principle of warrant requirement. This can serve as a guideline for investigative practice to develop in response to the advancement of the information society while efficiently fulfilling the role of discovering the substantive truth and also meeting the demand for protection of fundamental rights.

d. The relationship between expansion of participation-right guarantees and the ideal of discovering substantive truth

The criticism that, if the dissenting opinion is followed, confusion and burden will be imposed on investigative practice and another ideal of criminal justice, discovery of the substantive truth, may regress, is not correct. The scope of the guarantee of participation rights has already expanded to the substantive person subject to seizure by virtue of the legal doctrine of the 2016DO348 en banc decision. This doctrine is evaluated as having achieved a balance and harmony between the ideal of criminal justice that, in the seizure and search procedure of electronic information, the warrant requirement must be effectuated so as to guarantee the fundamental rights of the person subject to seizure concerning irrelevant information, and the other ideal of discovering substantive truth. It is true that law-enforcement agencies have come to bear a greater burden than before in determining the scope of participation-right guarantees, but such a circumstance cannot be described as a regression of the criminal justice ideal of discovering substantive truth. Criticizing the dissenting opinion, which sets the scope of the participation-right guarantee on the basis of the above legal doctrine, as causing a retreat in the discovery of substantive truth is no different from criticizing the 2016DO348 en banc decision on the same grounds.

The seizure and search practice of electronic information is being carried out in the form of imaging the digital storage medium on site, taking it out, and then searching and printing relevant information externally in a separate procedure. Since finding and seizing the tangible object of a digital storage medium at the scene is not greatly different from coercive investigation of traditional tangible objects, there is no additional restraint imposed on warrant-execution practice by expanding participation rights. The part where additional burden arises is in the imaging procedure and the procedure in which relevant information is separately searched and printed externally. However, because this part of the procedure is separately performed after the law-enforcement agency has securely secured the digital storage medium and the electronic information therein based on on-site presence and secrecy, etc., it is difficult to say that the expansion of participation rights creates additional obstacles to the on-site nature, speed, timeliness, and secrecy of the investigative procedure or burdens it to the degree that it would regress the criminal justice ideal of discovering substantive truth. Rather, the majority concurring opinion, by invoking the efficiency of investigative procedure and discovery of substantive truth, is causing the principle of warrant requirement and due process, which are demanded for the protection of the fundamental rights of individuals and businesses in a highly developed information society, to regress.

e. Participation-right issues arising from concealment of digital storage media, etc.

When the law-enforcement agency investigating the principal offender’s facts suspected of crime traces the whereabouts of the principal offender’s concealed digital storage medium and ultimately secures it from a third party who concealed evidence, is the principal offender not guaranteed participation rights in the search and printing process? Is it not a distortion of the fundamental purpose of the participation-right doctrine established by precedent to apply it so formally that it is sufficient to guarantee participation rights only to the third party, the evidence concealer? In such a situation, is there any device that ensures constitutional control over the execution of the warrant other than guaranteeing the principal offender’s participation rights? Is there any difference, for purposes of guaranteeing participation rights, between seizing a digital storage medium directly from the suspect and seizing it from a third party who received it from the suspect and concealed it? Are the intent to conceal evidence or the suspect status as a suspect for the crime of concealment of evidence on the part of the third party who concealed the digital storage medium an essential element in determining whether participation rights should be guaranteed to the principal offender? In all of these cases, should the principal offender, as the owner/manager of the digital storage medium, not still be regarded as having the interest in participation through exclusion of irrelevant information as the exclusive manager/disposer of the electronic information? From the perspective of participation rights, are the investigative procedure against the principal offender and the investigative procedure against the evidence concealer truly and substantively completely independent separate procedures, or is the latter substantially subsumed as part of the former? Since the principal offender and the evidence concealer each occupy the status of suspect while simultaneously and overlap-wise occupying the status of a third party with respect to the other party’s criminal suspicion, can each not become a subject to whom participation rights belong?

The structure of the principal offender and the evidence concealer contains a variety of issues for debate in determining the subject to whom participation rights belong. Focusing on these many special features, the dissenting opinion is the result of an effort to find answers to the above questions and, based on the precedents concerning the guarantee of participation rights, to determine the essence of participation rights and the core indicia of the subject to whom they belong. Based on the discussion developed by the dissenting opinion, I hope that this will provide an opportunity for active additional discussion on the scope and direction of participation-right guarantees in seizure and search procedures concerning digital storage media in an increasingly advanced information society.

For the foregoing reasons, I supplement the dissenting opinion."}

question: 신체의 liberty에 관한 explanations 중 which of the following are all incorrect? (다툼이 있는 경우 according to precedents) (a) 외국에서 형의 전부 또는 일부의 집행을 받은 자에 대하여 형을 감경 또는 면제할 수 있도록 한 statutory provision은 입법자의 legislative discretion의 범위 내에 속하므로 personal liberty를 침해하지 않는다. (b) punishment와는 달리, security measure는 행위자의 future risk of recidivism에 근거하는 것이고, security measure의 선고 여부는 행위시가 아니라 trial time의 재범위험성에 대한 판단에 따라 결정되므로, 어떤 security measure가 penal character가 강하고 personal liberty deprivation에 준하는 정도로 personal liberty를 제한하더라도 non-retroactivity principle of punishment은 적용되지 않는다. (c) Immigration Control Act에 따라 detained된 foreigners를 Habeas Corpus Act상 relief petition을 제기할 수 있는 detainees의 scope에서 제외하는 것은 Habeas Corpus Act에 따른 detention의 legality를 contest할 opportunity를 박탈하므로 personal liberty를 침해한다. (d) deportation order를 받은 person이 immediately outside the Republic of Korea로 deported될 수 없으면 deportation이 가능할 때까지 detention facility에 detained될 수 있도록 한 statutory provision은 administrative convenience와 uniformity만을 강조한 것으로 personal liberty를 침해한다. (e) counsel과 meet and communicate할 right는 constitutional provisions에 비추어 볼 때 arrest 또는 detention된 suspects or accused persons 자신에게만 limited되는 personal liberty에 관한 fundamental right이지, 그 provisions로부터 counsel의 arrested or detained suspect or accused person에 대한 meet and communicate right가 derived된다고 할 수는 없다.

Article 1(목적) 이 법은 Constitution이 보장하고 있는 국민의 fundamental rights를 보호하기 위하여 위법한 administrative disposition 또는 private person에 의한 facility commitment으로 인하여 부당하게 personal liberty를 제한당하고 있는 individual에 대한 relief procedures를 마련하는 것을 purpose로 한다.
인신보호법(Amended by Act No. 10364 on 2010. 6. 10.)
Article 3(Relief Petition) 피수용자에 대한 detention이 unlawfully commenced되거나 lawful detention 후 그 ground가 ceased to exist하였음에도 person이 still being detained인 때에는 피수용자 his or her statutory representative guardian spouse lineal relative sibling cohabitant employer 또는 detention facility의 person working at the detention facility(이하 “petitioner for relief”라 한다)는 이 법이 정하는 바에 따라 court에 relief를 petition할 수 있다. Provided, 다른 Act에 relief procedure가 있는 경우에는 reasonable period 내에 그 Act에 따라 relief를 obtain하는 것이 clearly impossible하여야 한다.
Immigration Control Act(Amended by Act No. 12421 on 2014. 3. 18.)
Article 46(Persons Subject to Deportation) ① 지방출입국ㆍ외국인관서의 장은 이 Chapter에 정한 procedures에 따라 다음 각 item의 어느 하나에 해당하는 foreigner를 Republic of Korea 밖으로 deport할 수 있다.
(Items omitted)
Article 51(Detention) ① immigration control officer는 외국인이 Article 46 paragraph 1의 각 item의 어느 하나에 해당한다고 suspect할 만한 reasonable grounds가 있고 flight risk가 있으면 local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head로부터 detention order를 obtain하여 그 foreigner를 detain할 수 있다.
③ urgent case에서 외국인이 Article 46 paragraph 1의 각 item의 어느 하나에 해당한다고 suspect할 만한 reasonable grounds가 있고 flight risk 또는 possibility of flight가 있으며 local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head로부터 detention order를 obtain할 time이 없을 때에는 immigration control officer는 그 reason을 inform하고 urgently detain할 수 있다.
Article 52(Period and Place of Detention) ① Article 51에 따라 detained된 foreigner가 deportation 대상자인지 examine하고 determine하기 위한 detention period는 10 days 이내로 한다. Provided, unavoidable reason이 있으면 local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head의 permission을 받아 10 days를 초과하지 않는 extent에서 only once 연장할 수 있다.
Article 55(Objection to Detention) ① detention order pursuant로 detained된 person 또는 his or her statutory representative 등은 local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head를 통해 Minister of Justice에게 objection to detention을 file할 수 있다.
② paragraph 1에 따른 objection을 받은 경우 Minister of Justice는 without delay relevant documents를 examine하여 objection이 without merit라고 found되면 decision으로 dismiss하고 reasoned라고 found되면 decision으로 detained person의 release from detention을 order하여야 한다.
③ paragraph 2에 따른 decision 전에 Minister of Justice는 필요하면 persons concerned의 statements를 hear할 수 있다.
Article 63(Detention and Release from Detention of a Person Who Has Received a Deportation Order) ① local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head는 deportation order를 received한 person을 passport가 없거나 transportation secured되지 아니하는 등의 reasons로 즉시 Republic of Korea 밖으로 repatriate할 수 없으면 repatriate할 수 있을 때까지 그 person을 detention facility에 detain할 수 있다.
② paragraph 1에 따라 detaining하는 경우 그 period가 3 months를 exceed하면 local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head는 every 3 months prior approval을 Minister of Justice로부터 obtain하여야 한다.
③ local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head가 paragraph 2의 approval을 obtain하지 못하면 without delay 그 person을 release from detention하여야 한다.
④ deportation order를 received한 person이 another country로부터 entry denied되는 등의 reasons로 repatriated될 수 없음이 clear하게 된 경우에는 local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head는 그 person을 release from detention할 수 있다.
⑤ local immigration office 또는 foreigners' office의 head가 paragraph 3 또는 4에 따라 person을 release from detention하는 경우에는 residence restriction이나 other necessary conditions를 attach할 수 있다.
⑥ paragraph 1에 따른 detention의 경우 Articles 53 through 55, Articles 56-2 through 56-9, and Article 57 shall apply mutatis mutandis.
Immigration Control Act(Amended by Act No. 10282 on 2010. 5. 14.)
Article 51(Detention) ② paragraph 1에 따른 detention order issuance를 apply할 때에는 detention necessity를 establish할 수 있는 materials를 attach하고 submit하여야 한다.
④ immigration control officer는 paragraph 3에 따라 foreigner를 urgently detain하면 immediately emergency detention notice를 prepare하여 그 foreigner에게 show하여야 한다.
⑤ immigration control officer는 paragraph 3에 따라 foreigner를 detain한 경우에는 48 hours 이내에 detention order를 obtain하여 foreigner에게 show하여야 하며 detention order를 obtain하지 못한 경우에는 detention이 immediately released되어야 한다.
Article 52(Period and Place of Detention) ② detention이 made될 수 있는 places는 foreigner detention room foreigner detention center 또는 Minister of Justice가 designated하는 other place(이하 “detention facility”라 한다)로 한다."}

{"[2013HEONMA129]": "The 청구인은 대구지방검찰청 포항지청 2012형제15580호 상해 사건에 관하여 피청구인이 2012. 11. 30. 결정한 기소유예의 불기소처분이 헌법상 보장된 청구인의 평등권 등 기본권을 침해한다며 그 취소를 구하는 this constitutional complaint case를 filed하였다.

However, even upon close examination of the record of this case, it does not appear that the Respondent가 위 사건에 관해 현저히 형평에 반하는 수사를 하였거나, 헌법의 해석, 법률의 적용 또는 증거판단에 있어 불기소처분의 결정에 영향을 미친 중대한 잘못이 있었다고 보이지 아니하고, 달리 피청구인의 이 사건 처분이 헌법재판소가 관여할 정도로 자의적 처분이라고 볼 자료도 없으므로, it cannot be said that 청구인이 주장하는 기본권이 infringed thereby.

Accordingly, since the petition for adjudication in this case is without merit, it is decided to dismiss it, and the decision is made as stated in the Order, by the unanimous opinion of all participating Justices.

{"[2015HEONMA1204]": "1. 사건개요
A. Suspect Yun XX-hyeon was arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant at around 19:00 on 2015. 10. 5., and a detention warrant was sought. 청구인, an attorney, was entrusted by the family of the above suspect and, after inquiring by telephone at around 17:00 on 2015. 10. 6. to the Respondent prosecutor of the XX District Prosecutors’ Office who was investigating the case (hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent Prosecutor”) whether a counsel visitation was possible, visited prosecutor’s office room No. XX at the XX District Prosecutors’ Office at around 19:00 on the same day, carrying a visitation application, and applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for a counsel visitation.
B. The Respondent correctional officer of the XX Detention Center who was in charge of escorting the above suspect (hereinafter referred to as the “Respondent Correctional Officer”) received custody of the above suspect from the Respondent Prosecutor’s office at around 17:00 on the same day and kept him waiting in the detention room within the Prosecutors’ Office, and then, at around 19:10 on the same day, upon receiving a request from the Respondent Prosecutor to summon the suspect for night questioning, brought the above suspect into the prosecutor’s office.
C. The Respondent Prosecutor informed the Respondent Correctional Officer that the Claimant had made an application for visitation, and the Respondent Correctional Officer, after inquiring with the official in charge of counsel visitation at the XX Detention Center regarding the procedures for handling it, informed the Claimant that, pursuant to Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, counsel visitation could not be permitted because the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials (“09:00 to 18:00”) had elapsed.
D. Thereafter, the Respondent Prosecutor took no further action regarding the Claimant’s application for visitation, and the Claimant remained in the prosecutor’s office but ultimately left without having visited the above suspect. After the Claimant left, the Respondent Prosecutor continued questioning the above suspect, and the Claimant was not retained as counsel for the above suspect.
E. The Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint on 2015. 12. 28., alleging that the acts of the Respondents in denying the application for counsel visitation, and Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners, which the Respondent Correctional Officer relied upon as the legal basis therefor, infringed his fundamental rights.

2. 심판대상
The subject matter of this case is whether: ① the acts of the Respondents in failing to take measures to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect Yun XX-hyeon at prosecutor’s office room No. XX of the XX District Prosecutors’ Office at around 19:00 on 2015. 10. 6. (hereinafter, the Respondent Prosecutor’s denial of visitation shall be referred to as the “Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case,” the Respondent Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation shall be referred to as the “Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case,” and these acts collectively as the “denial of visitation in this case”), and ② Article 58(1) of the Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (wholly amended by Presidential Decree No. 21095 on 2008. 10. 29.; hereinafter referred to as the “Visitation Hours Provision in this case”) infringe the Claimant’s fundamental rights (hereinafter, the “Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners” shall be referred to as the “Execution of Sentences Act”).
The provision subject to adjudication and related provisions are as follows:

[Provision Subject to Adjudication]
Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (wholly amended by Presidential Decree No. 21095 on 2008. 10. 29.)
Article 58 (Visitation) (1) Visitation by a prisoner shall take place every day (excluding public holidays and days designated by the Minister of Justice) within working hours pursuant to Article 9 of the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials.

[Related Provisions]
Criminal Procedure Act (enacted by Act No. 341 on 1954. 9. 23.)
Article 34 (Visitation, Communication, and Medical Treatment with Defendant or Suspect) A defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint and may exchange documents or articles with him or her, and may have a physician provide treatment.

Criminal Procedure Act (amended by Act No. 8496 on 2007. 6. 1.)
Article 243-2 (Participation of Defense Counsel, etc.) (1) A prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground.
(2) to (5) Omitted

Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (wholly amended by Act No. 8728 on 2007. 12. 21.)
Article 3 (Scope of Application) This Act applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required.

Enforcement Decree of the Act on the Execution of Sentences and Treatment of Prisoners (amended by Presidential Decree No. 25397 on 2014. 6. 25.)
Article 58 (Visitation) (1) Omitted
(2) Except for untried prisoners who visit with defense counsel (including persons intending to become defense counsel; the same shall apply hereinafter), the visitation time for prisoners shall be limited to not more than 30 minutes per visit.
(3) The number of visits by prisoners shall be four times per month.
(4) Visitation by prisoners shall take place in a place equipped with contact-blocking facilities; provided, however, that this shall not apply in any of the following cases:
1. Where an untried prisoner (including a convicted prisoner under investigation or trial in a criminal case and a person sentenced to death whose sentence has become final and conclusive) visits with defense counsel
2. Where a prisoner visits with an attorney who is a representative in a litigation case, and where there is no risk of undermining the safety or order of the correctional institution
(5) Except for the matters prescribed in the Act and this Decree, necessary matters concerning the number, time, place, etc. of visits by prisoners other than convicted prisoners, persons sentenced to death, and untried prisoners shall be determined by the Minister of Justice.
(6) If necessary in order to perform affairs concerning the visitation of prisoners by persons outside the correctional institution, the warden may process data containing a resident registration number, passport number, driver’s license number, or alien registration number pursuant to Article 19 of the Enforcement Decree of the Personal Information Protection Act.

Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials (amended by Presidential Decree No. 23010 on 2011. 7. 4.)
Article 9 (Working Hours, etc.) (1) The weekly working hours of public officials shall be 40 hours excluding lunch time, and Saturdays shall, in principle, be days off.
(2) The daily working hours of public officials shall be from 9:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m., and lunch time shall be from 12:00 noon to 1:00 p.m.; provided, however, that if the head of an administrative agency deems it necessary in consideration of the nature of the duties, the region, or the special characteristics of the institution, he or she may set lunch time differently within the range of one hour.
(3), (4) Omitted

3. 청구인의 주장
A. The Claimant was unable to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon due to the Respondents’ denial of visitation in this case, and as a result, lost the opportunity to assist the above suspect, and direct disadvantage was caused to the exercise of the above suspect’s right of defense. The denial of visitation in this case infringed not only the above suspect’s right of access and communication with counsel, but also the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right of access and communication with counsel.
B. Since a detention warrant is sought within 48 hours after a suspect is arrested, the right of a suspect to immediately receive assistance from counsel must be guaranteed during that period as well, and considering that the period immediately before the warrant review hearing is the time when the assistance of counsel is most needed, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which limits counsel visitation hours to public officials’ working hours, violates the principle of prohibition against excessive restriction and infringes the Claimant’s right of access and communication with counsel.
Moreover, where an arrested suspect is housed in a police detention cell, Article 7(1) of the Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc. and Article 37(1) of the Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects apply, so that counsel visitation is permitted even outside the working hours under the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials. Accordingly, because an unreasonable discrimination arises in the exercise of defense counsel’s right of access and communication depending on whether the suspect is confined in a detention center or housed in a detention cell, the Visitation Hours Provision in this case infringes the Claimant’s right to equality.

4. 피의자/피고인과 변호인의 접견교통 제도
A. Constitutional Basis
The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution provides that “any person who is arrested or detained shall have the right to prompt assistance of counsel.” The Constitutional Court has held: “Even in the case of a suspect who is not detained, the right to the assistance of counsel is a natural content recognized under the constitutional principles of a rule-of-law state and due process contained in our Constitution, and Article 12(4) of the Constitution also separately and expressly provides for this in order to particularly emphasize the importance of the right to the assistance of counsel for persons under physical restraint.” (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138). In this manner, a suspect or defendant (hereinafter, “suspect or defendant” shall be referred to as “suspect, etc.”) is recognized as having the right to the assistance of counsel regardless of whether he or she is arrested or detained.
In order for a suspect, etc. to sufficiently exercise the right of defense, he or she must be able to consult sufficiently on all factual and legal issues through visitation and communication with defense counsel or a “person who intends to become defense counsel” (hereinafter, defense counsel or a “person who intends to become defense counsel” shall be referred to as “defense counsel, etc.”). With respect to visitation and communication between a suspect, etc. and defense counsel, etc., matters are provided in Article 34 and Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act, Article 84(1) and (2), and Article 85 of the Execution of Sentences Act, etc., and these provisions concretize the right to the assistance of counsel guaranteed by the Constitution as above. Among them, Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that a “person who intends to become defense counsel” also has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc.

B. ‘신체구속’ 및 ‘변호인이 되려는 자’의 의미
(1) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel may visit a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint.” Here, “a defendant or suspect who is under physical restraint” means not only a suspect, etc. detained pursuant to a detention warrant, but also a suspect, etc. arrested pursuant to an arrest warrant or arrested by emergency arrest or as a person caught in flagrante delicto, and it should be understood to presuppose deprivation of physical liberty in whatever form.
(2) Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act expressly provides that not only defense counsel but also a “person who intends to become defense counsel” has the right to visit and communicate with a suspect, etc. Here, “a person who intends to become defense counsel” should be understood to include not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment of defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own. It is difficult to say that, in a state where physical liberty is suppressed and communication with the outside is severed, a suspect, etc. can decide and carry through his or her own intention without being conscious of investigative authorities, and if the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” were permitted only when the suspect, etc. expressly indicates an intention to receive the assistance of counsel, this could result in the existence of the right of visitation and communication being substantially determined by the will of the investigative authorities.
The Supreme Court, in a case where an attorney not appointed as defense counsel expressed an intention to exercise the right of visitation and communication with respect to a suspect arrested, but it was not confirmed what the suspect’s intention was, held that “even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a ‘defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel’ as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act” (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.).

C. Subject Authorized to Determine Whether to Permit Visitation
The Execution of Sentences Act aims to promote the correction and rehabilitation of convicted prisoners and their sound return to society, and to prescribe matters necessary concerning the treatment and rights of prisoners and the operation of correctional institutions (Article 1). Accordingly, Part II of the Execution of Sentences Act regulates the treatment of prisoners, and matters concerning the treatment of prisoners, such as confinement of prisoners, visitation, exchange of correspondence and telephone communication, maintenance of safety and order, discipline and rewards/punishments, and special protection for female prisoners and pregnant women, are vested in the authority of the heads of prisons and detention centers. Meanwhile, the Execution of Sentences Act is a statute that applies to the premises of correctional institutions and to other places where correctional officers are guarding prisoners and where the control of correctional officers is required (Article 3). In light of the legislative purpose, regulatory content, scope of application, etc. of the Execution of Sentences Act, when there is an application for visitation by a prisoner, this concerns a matter of treatment of prisoners; therefore, if the place is a space where the guarding and control of prisoners by correctional officers is required, it is in principle the warden of the prison or detention center, or the correctional officer entrusted by such warden, who determines whether to permit it.
However, Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “a prosecutor or judicial police officer shall, upon application by a suspect or his or her defense counsel, legal representative, spouse, lineal relative, brother, or sister, allow defense counsel to visit the suspect or allow defense counsel to participate in the interrogation of the suspect unless there is a justifiable ground,” thereby establishing a special provision to the above principle and making the prosecutor or judicial police officer determine whether to permit such visitation when there is an application for visitation by defense counsel during the interrogation of a suspect.
Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act, however, regulates the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel and the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” without making any distinction between them; therefore, even where a “person who intends to become defense counsel” applies for visitation pursuant to Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act during the interrogation of a suspect, the subject who determines whether to permit it should also be the prosecutor or judicial police officer, and such interpretation is consistent with the content of Article 243-2(1) of the Criminal Procedure Act.

5. 적법요건 충족 여부에 대한 판단
A. Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case
(1) 존재 여부
A constitutional complaint may be filed when fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution are infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power (Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act); therefore, in order to file a constitutional complaint, there must first be a fact of “exercise or non-exercise of public power” that caused the infringement of fundamental rights, and where there is no fact at all of exercise or non-exercise of public power that is subject to constitutional complaint, the petition is unlawful (see Constitutional Court 2004. 11. 25. 2004HEONMA178; Constitutional Court 2014. 3. 31. 2014HEONMA239).
Here, as seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor merely informed the correctional officer of the fact that the Claimant had applied for visitation, and even though the Claimant continued to stay in the prosecutor’s office in order to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon after the correctional officer in charge denied visitation between the Claimant and the suspect, the Respondent Prosecutor did not take measures such as allowing the visitation to take place in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room.
Since the Respondent Prosecutor’s failure to take any further measures after the correctional officer’s notice of denial of visitation can be assessed as substantially equivalent to denying the Claimant’s application for visitation (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181; Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.), the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case exists as an exercise of public power subject to a constitutional complaint.
(2) Whether the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized - Whether the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” can be regarded as a constitutional fundamental right
(a) Organization of the issue
Because the Claimant was not appointed as defense counsel for suspect Yun XX-hyeon, with respect to the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, only whether the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” was infringed is at issue.
A constitutional complaint is a system by which a “person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed” petitions the Constitutional Court for adjudication in order to obtain relief from that infringement; therefore, for the constitutional complaint against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case to be lawful, the right allegedly infringed by the Claimant, namely the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” must not only be recognized as a statutory right but must further be recognized as a constitutional fundamental right.
(b) Constitutional Court precedents
The Constitutional Court, in its decision rendered on 2003. 3. 27., 2000HEONMA474, for the first time recognized the core part of the right to assistance of counsel as a constitutional fundamental right, and also took the same position in its decision 2016HEONMA503 rendered on 2017. 11. 30.; the gist of the decision 2016HEONMA503 is as follows:
“[T]he right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can be concretely realized in the mutual relationship between them and defense counsel. The right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel can become solid through the guarantee of the right of defense counsel to assist them, whereas if the right of defense counsel is not guaranteed, it may become a mere empty shell. The core part of the right of defense counsel to assist a suspect or defendant, without which it becomes a dead letter for them to receive the assistance of counsel, stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel. Therefore, in order to practically secure the right of a suspect and defendant to receive the assistance of counsel, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect and defendant must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.”
(c) Determination
1) Article 27(4) of the Constitution provides that “a criminal defendant shall be presumed innocent until a conviction becomes final and conclusive,” thereby declaring the principle of presumption of innocence. This principle of presumption of innocence originates from the constitutional ideal that has the respect for human dignity as its ultimate goal and seeks to protect the status of suspects, etc., who are in an unfavorable position, so that their disadvantages in criminal proceedings are limited to the minimum necessary. Detention is a system recognized only when there are especially unavoidable reasons with respect to suspects, etc., but the detention system is susceptible to abuse by investigative or trial authorities merely for the convenience of investigation or trial, and while in a detained state, the right to remain silent prescribed in Article 12(2) of the Constitution may not be effectively guaranteed. Accordingly, in order to remove the various harms arising from the situation of physical restraint with respect to suspects, etc. who are presumed innocent and to ensure that detention is not improperly used beyond its original purpose, the main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution guarantees as a fundamental right the right of a person under physical restraint to receive the assistance of counsel as stated above (see Constitutional Court 1995. 7. 21. 92HEONMA144).
The reason for and necessity of recognizing, as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a detained suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel applies equally to arrested suspects, etc.
2) The main text of Article 12(4) of the Constitution clearly provides that, upon being arrested or detained, a person has the right to prompt assistance of counsel, thereby making clear that suspects, etc. have the right to receive the assistance of counsel even before counsel is appointed. The right of a suspect, etc. who has not yet appointed defense counsel to receive the assistance of counsel is concretized through the appointment of defense counsel; the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel is the starting point and the most basic component of the right to receive the assistance of counsel, and is a right that cannot even be limited by law (see Constitutional Court 2004. 9. 23. 2000HEONMA138). Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication with a “person who intends to become defense counsel” that a suspect, etc. has for purposes of appointing defense counsel must also be protected as a constitutional fundamental right.
3) In order for a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel, a relationship of trust must be formed between the suspect, etc. and the “person who intends to become defense counsel,” and for this purpose, sufficient consultation must be conducted through visitation and communication with the “person who intends to become defense counsel.” In this way, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is intended to solidify the right of a suspect, etc. to appoint defense counsel and receive assistance from that counsel; if it is not guaranteed, the right of the suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from defense counsel through the appointment of counsel will inevitably become meaningless. Accordingly, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is a core part for assisting a suspect, etc., and stands in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the constitutional fundamental right of the suspect, etc. to visit and communicate with a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”
4) Therefore, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” as a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., must also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right in order to practically secure the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of a “person who intends to become defense counsel.” Accordingly, this part of the petition seeking a constitutional determination on the ground that the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case infringed the Claimant’s constitutional fundamental right, namely the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” also satisfies the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.
(3) Whether an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is recognized
A constitutional complaint must be filed only after all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act); however, where the claimant failed to take a prior remedy procedure due to a mistake based on justifiable grounds not attributable to his or her disadvantage, or where there is little possibility that the right will be remedied through the prior remedy procedure, or where it is objectively uncertain whether the right-concretization procedure is permitted, making it impossible to expect performance of the prior remedy procedure, it is recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity (see Constitutional Court 1989. 9. 4. 88HEONMA22; Constitutional Court 2008. 5. 29. 2007HEONMA712, etc.).
However, since the subject who finally determines the Claimant’s application for visitation with suspect Yun XX-hyeon is the Respondent Prosecutor, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case falls under “dispositions concerning detention by a prosecutor and dispositions concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2” that are subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without first filing a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act.
The Supreme Court, however, has held that even a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of a denial of visitation by an investigative agency must have a legal interest, and that where the purpose sought to be achieved through the quasi-appeal during the pendency of the case has already been achieved or where the interest has been lost due to the lapse of time or other circumstances, the quasi-appeal becomes unlawful for lack of interest (see Supreme Court Decision 98MO121 dated 1999. 6. 14.; Supreme Court Decision 2014MO686 dated 2014. 4. 15.), yet has not presented specific criteria therefor. Accordingly, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, which ended on the day of the incident, it is objectively uncertain whether the court would deem legal interest to be lacking or would proceed to a merits determination, and thus this is a case where it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure.
Accordingly, this part of the petition should be recognized as a lawful petition as an exception to subsidiarity.
(4) Sub-conclusion
As above, the petition concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case targets an exercise of public power subject to constitutional complaint, the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights is recognized, an exception to the principle of subsidiarity is also recognized, and all other requirements for lawfulness are satisfied; thus, it is lawful.

B. The Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case
Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act limits the subject matter of constitutional complaints to acts of public power by providing that a person whose fundamental rights have been infringed by the “exercise or non-exercise of public power” may file a constitutional complaint.
According to the record, at the time of the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case, the Respondent Prosecutor handed over the physical custody of suspect Yun XX-hyeon to the Respondent Correctional Officer so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but it is recognized that an interrogation of the suspect was scheduled even at night, and thus it may be said that the interrogation of the above suspect was ongoing. In addition, the Claimant at that time applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for counsel visitation.
As seen above, where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect, the prosecutor or judicial police officer must determine whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that a correctional officer who escorted the suspect to the investigative agency is not vested with the authority to permit or restrict such visitation.
Article 118 of the “Operational Guidelines on the Management of Prisoners” (Ministerial Instruction of the Ministry of Justice No. 1077, 2015. 1. 13.), which was in force at the time of this case, provided that where there is an application for defense counsel visitation with a prisoner outside the institution who is being escorted out, the escorting correctional officer is to conduct the visitation between the escorted prisoner and defense counsel through certain procedures, such as obtaining permission from the warden. However, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center, or a correctional officer delegated by them, determines whether to permit it, and cannot be said to apply to cases, such as this one, where an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. is made during the interrogation of a suspect, and the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it.
Ultimately, in this case, because it cannot be said that the Respondent Correctional Officer had the authority to determine whether to permit visitation between the Claimant and suspect Yun XX-hyeon, the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case does not constitute an “exercise of public power” that is made subject to constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act.

C. The Visitation Hours Provision in this case
The main text of Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act provides that “a person whose fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may ... file a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court,” which means that only a person whose own fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution have been currently and directly infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power may file a constitutional complaint. Therefore, if the exercise of public power has no effect whatsoever on the legal status of the person seeking to file a constitutional complaint, then there is no possibility or danger of infringement of fundamental rights in the first place, and filing a constitutional complaint against such exercise of public power is not permitted (see Constitutional Court 1999. 5. 27. 97HEONMA368; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2012HEONMA630, etc.).
The Visitation Hours Provision in this case is a provision that applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and it cannot be said to apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it; accordingly, it must be said that the denial or restriction of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect cannot be based on that provision. In practice as well, the police and prosecutors impose no time restrictions whatsoever on visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect [see Article 7 of the “Rules on Defense Counsel Visitation and Participation, etc.” (Korean National Police Agency Instruction No. 882, 2018. 8. 13.), Article 37(2) of the “Rules on Detention and Escort of Suspects” (Korean National Police Agency Instruction No. 883, 2018. 8. 13.), Article 2(6) and Article 8 of the “Guidelines on the Operation of Defense Counsel Participation in Suspect Interrogation” (Korean Supreme Prosecutors’ Office guidelines, amended 2017. 12. 4.), and Article 230 of the “Guidelines on Defense Counsel Visitation and Communication with Suspects” (Seoul Central District Prosecutors’ Office Rule No. 230, 2017. 8. 30.)].
As seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation with suspect Yun XX-hyeon, against whom interrogation was continuing, and therefore the Visitation Hours Provision in this case does not apply here, nor did the Respondent Prosecutor at the time deny the above visitation application by applying that provision. Accordingly, this part of the petition lacks self-relatedness for purposes of the possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.

6. 이 사건 검사의 접견불허행위의 기본권 침해 여부에 대한 판단
A. Whether the Claimant’s right of access and communication was restricted
As seen above, the Claimant applied to the Respondent Prosecutor for visitation and remained in the prosecutor’s office, but due to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ultimately could not visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon and left the prosecutor’s office; accordingly, it is reasonable to view the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as having restricted the Claimant’s right of access and communication with the above suspect.
However, according to the record, suspect Yun XX-hyeon did not raise an objection to the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, visited with another attorney twice the following day, and that attorney personally appeared and responded at the pre-detention suspect interrogation hearing. Nevertheless, even if the suspect did not indicate an intention to visit and communicate with a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” if a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, visitation with the suspect must be permitted (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.); moreover, the Claimant had even been entrusted by suspect Yun XX-hyeon’s family and intended to visit the suspect, so at the time of the visitation application there was sufficient possibility that the Claimant would become defense counsel for the above suspect; and the person claiming infringement of fundamental rights caused by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is not suspect Yun XX-hyeon but the Claimant. In light of these circumstances, the facts recognized above are not factors to be considered in determining whether the Claimant’s fundamental rights were infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case.

B. Whether the Claimant’s visitation application was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication
Because the right of access and communication of defense counsel, etc. must be exercised within the limits that do not infringe the original purpose of the physical restraint system, attempts by defense counsel, etc. to visit a suspect, etc. beyond the limits that can realistically be guaranteed in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances do not constitute a proper exercise of the right of access and communication and cannot be permitted (see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO657 dated 2007. 1. 31.; Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.).
However, in this case, since suspect Yun XX-hyeon was scheduled to continue being interrogated at night on that day, it appears that measures could have been taken to permit visitation and communication between the Claimant and the above suspect in the prosecutor’s office or in a separately prepared counsel visitation room before the interrogation, and thus in light of the concrete temporal and spatial circumstances at the time of the visitation application, no specific circumstances are discernible showing that the Claimant, who intended to become defense counsel, attempted to abuse the exercise of visitation and communication with the suspect beyond the limits realistically guaranteeable or beyond the original purpose of the physical restraint system.
Accordingly, the Claimant’s visitation application must be deemed to have been exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”

C. Whether it was based on the Constitution or statutes
(1) In the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc., “free visitation,” that is, “visitation in which confidentiality regarding the content of the conversation is fully guaranteed and the parties may converse freely without any restriction, influence, pressure, or improper interference,” is not of a nature that can be restricted under any pretext (see Constitutional Court 1992. 1. 28. 91HEONMA111). However, this means only that such is the case where visitation actually takes place between a person arrested or detained and defense counsel, etc.; it does not mean that no restriction whatsoever may be imposed on visitation itself with defense counsel, etc. The right to the assistance of counsel and the right of visitation and communication with counsel, which is one component thereof, may, like all other constitutional fundamental rights, be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law when necessary for national security, maintenance of order, or public welfare (see Constitutional Court 2011. 5. 26. 2009HEONMA341; Constitutional Court 2016. 4. 28. 2015HEONMA243), and the same shall apply to the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel.”
(2) As seen above, the Respondent Prosecutor temporarily handed over the physical custody of suspect Yun XX-hyeon to the correctional officer in charge so that he could have dinner and rest in the detention room, but since a night interrogation of the above suspect was planned, it may be said that the investigation or interrogation of the above suspect was continuing.
Although the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel, etc. may be restricted not only by the Constitution but also by law, neither the Constitution nor laws such as the Criminal Procedure Act contain a provision allowing restriction or refusal where there is an application for visitation by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect. This is to ensure, in light of the importance of the right of access and communication held by a suspect, etc., that the right of access and communication held by defense counsel, etc. is also guaranteed to the maximum extent.
The Visitation Hours Provision in this case, which is delegated by Article 41(4) of the Execution of Sentences Act, restricts visitation and communication between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. by limiting visitation by prisoners to working hours pursuant to the Regulations on the Service of National Public Officials; however, as seen above, that provision applies to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. where the warden of the prison or detention center determines whether to permit it, and does not apply to cases of visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. during the interrogation of a suspect where the prosecutor or judicial police officer determines whether to permit it, and thus it must be said that visitation applications by defense counsel, etc. cannot be denied or restricted on the basis of that provision.
Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes.

D. Sub-conclusion
Ultimately, the Claimant’s visitation application concerning suspect Yun XX-hyeon was exercised within the scope of the right of access and communication guaranteed to a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” and furthermore the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case was made without the basis of the Constitution or statutes; therefore, it infringed the Claimant’s right of access and communication.

7. 결론
Accordingly, the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case should be found unconstitutional and revoked; however, since the denial of visitation has already ended, we shall, for declaratory purposes and to prevent repetition of the same or similar infringement of fundamental rights, make a determination that it is unconstitutional. The petition regarding the Correctional Officer’s denial of visitation in this case and the Visitation Hours Provision in this case is unlawful in its entirety and shall therefore be dismissed, and it is so decided as stated in the order. The concurrence of the remaining participating Justices was reached, except for the dissenting opinion by Justices Cho Yong-ho, Lee Eun-ae, and Lee Jong-seok regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case as stated in Section 8 below.

8. 재판관 조용호, 이은애, 이종석의 반대의견
We are of the view that the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is also unlawful and should be dismissed, and we state our opinion as follows.

A. 가능성 of infringement of fundamental rights
(1) A constitutional complaint under Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act may be filed only by a person whose “fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution” have been infringed by the exercise or non-exercise of public power. Therefore, a constitutional complaint alleging infringement of a right based merely on statute, rather than on a constitutional fundamental right, is unlawful.
(2) In the Constitutional Court’s decision 2012HEONMA610 rendered on 2015. 7. 30., three Justices presented the following separate opinion:
“Guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel means sufficiently and substantively guaranteeing the activities of defense counsel aimed at assisting the person arrested, etc. Thus, the Criminal Procedure Act recognizes, as concrete means for substantively guaranteeing the right to the assistance of counsel, the right of visitation and communication of defense counsel (Article 34), defense counsel’s right to inspect and copy investigative and litigation records (Articles 35 and 266-3), and defense counsel’s right to participate in various procedures such as investigation and trial (Articles 121, 163, 243-2, etc.).
The reason special rights such as the right to inspect and copy records or the right of visitation and communication are recognized for defense counsel is that they all originate from the purpose of faithfully guaranteeing the right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel, and it cannot be viewed as a right recognized in order to guarantee defense counsel’s own fundamental rights. Defense counsel exercises the ‘right to assist as defense counsel’ recognized in the Criminal Procedure Act for the benefit of the person arrested, etc. as an assistant to the person arrested, etc., not for the protection of his or her own fundamental rights. Therefore, the ‘right to assist as defense counsel’ should be viewed as a statutory right recognized as a result of the legislator concretely shaping it through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act in order to faithfully guarantee the constitutional fundamental right of a person arrested, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel.
From this perspective, the Constitutional Court has long held that the constitutional right of visitation and communication with defense counsel is a fundamental right concerning personal liberty limited only to suspects and defendants, and that defense counsel’s own right of visitation and communication with a suspect or defendant cannot be regarded as a constitutional right, but is merely a right guaranteed only by Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act; accordingly, it dismissed a constitutional complaint filed by defense counsel on the ground that there was no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 1991. 7. 8. 89HEONMA181).”
For the reasons stated in the above separate opinion, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” is also merely a statutory right specifically formed through individual statutes such as the Criminal Procedure Act as an indirect and incidental effect arising from recognizing the “right to receive the assistance of counsel” of a person arrested, etc. as a fundamental right, and cannot be viewed as an “independent fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution.”
(3) The majority opinion relies on the Court’s majority opinions in Constitutional Court 2000HEONMA474 decided on 2003. 3. 27. and Constitutional Court 2016HEONMA503 decided on 2017. 11. 30., which held that “in order for the right of a suspect, etc. to receive the assistance of counsel to be practically secured, the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist the suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right,” and reasons that the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” should also be guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right because it is a core right for assisting a suspect, etc., and if it is not guaranteed, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless.
It is true that through visitation counsel can grasp the status of a detained suspect, etc. and devise appropriate responses accordingly, explain the meaning of the facts of suspicion or the charges, consult about countermeasures by hearing the opinions of the suspect, etc. thereon, and provide comfort to a suspect, etc. who is in a legally and psychologically anxious state, thereby restoring psychological stability and enabling the suspect, etc. to effectively exercise the right of defense within the criminal procedure (see Constitutional Court 2009. 10. 29. 2007HEONMA992). It is also true that through visitation and communication between a “person who intends to become defense counsel” and a suspect, etc., such advice, consultation, and comfort to the suspect, etc. are possible to some extent. However, when a “person who intends to become defense counsel” visits and communicates with a suspect, etc., because the point at which it is confirmed whether the suspect, etc. will actually retain the attorney and receive assistance from him or her has not yet been reached, the main purpose may be seen as the person’s own retention activities rather than assistance to the suspect, etc.; and the disadvantage suffered by the “person who intends to become defense counsel” due to inability to visit the suspect, etc., namely the disadvantage resulting from failure to obtain a criminal case retention, is merely an indirect, factual, and economic interest (see Constitutional Court 2004. 4. 29. 2002HEONMA756).
Meanwhile, as stated by the majority opinion, it is reasonable to view not only a person who has been requested to be appointed as defense counsel but has not yet filed a notice of appointment as defense counsel, but also a person who seeks to act as defense counsel on his or her own, as falling within the meaning of “a person who intends to become defense counsel,” and the Supreme Court has also held that “even where a person who has expressed an intention to become defense counsel is objectively recognized as having a possibility of becoming defense counsel, he or she may not be restricted from visiting a defendant or suspect under physical restraint on the ground that he or she is not a ‘defense counsel or a person who intends to become defense counsel’ as prescribed in Article 34 of the Criminal Procedure Act” (see Supreme Court 2013DO16162 decided on 2017. 3. 9.). If the meaning of “a person who intends to become defense counsel” is interpreted as above, the right of visitation and communication of such a person should be viewed as a right recognized to that person regardless of the suspect’s or defendant’s will, at the stage before assisting the suspect, etc.
In light of the above circumstances, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” cannot be viewed as standing in a relationship of mutual complementarity with the right of a suspect, etc. to receive assistance, and it cannot be concluded that, unless it is elevated and guaranteed as a constitutional fundamental right, the right of a suspect, etc. to receive sufficient assistance from counsel becomes meaningless. Therefore, even if one adopts the view that the core part of defense counsel’s right to assist a suspect, etc. must be protected as a constitutional fundamental right, there is no need, as in the majority opinion, to understand the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel” as well as a constitutional fundamental right.
(4) Ultimately, the right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be regarded as a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution; accordingly, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint against the denial of visitation is unlawful because there is no possibility of infringement of fundamental rights.

B. Subsidiarity
(1) Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act provides that “if there is an objection to a disposition concerning detention, seizure, or the return of seized articles made by a prosecutor or judicial police officer, or to a disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc. under Article 243-2, a petition may be filed with the court having jurisdiction over the place where the duties are performed, or with the court corresponding to the prosecutor’s public prosecutors’ office to which the prosecutor belongs, for revocation or alteration of the disposition.”
An act by an investigative agency denying visitation between a suspect and defense counsel, etc. falls under a “disposition concerning detention” or a “disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc.” subject to quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, and therefore not only the suspect or defense counsel but also a “person who intends to become defense counsel” may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal pursuant to that provision (see Supreme Court Decision 89MO37 dated 1990. 2. 13.; Supreme Court Decision 91MO24 dated 1991. 3. 28.; Supreme Court Decision 2006MO656 dated 2007. 1. 31., etc.).
A constitutional complaint may not be filed unless all procedures have been exhausted where there is a remedy procedure under other laws (proviso to Article 68(1) of the Constitutional Court Act), and the Constitutional Court has held that where a constitutional complaint is filed without going through such a procedure despite the availability of a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, it is unlawful for failure to exhaust the lawful remedy procedure prescribed by other laws (see Constitutional Court 2007. 5. 31. 2006HEONMA1131).
(2) The Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case constitutes a “disposition concerning detention” or a “disposition concerning a defense counsel’s participation, etc.” subject to a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act. Nevertheless, the Claimant filed the present constitutional complaint without seeking revocation or alteration of the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case through the quasi-appeal procedure.
The majority opinion held that, because the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case ended on the day of the incident, if the Claimant were to file a quasi-appeal seeking revocation thereof, it would be objectively uncertain whether the court would proceed to a merits determination, and thus it is difficult to expect the Claimant to have exhausted the prior remedy procedure; on that basis, it concluded that the constitutional complaint concerning the denial of visitation was lawful as an exception to subsidiarity.
However, after the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, the Claimant was unable to visit suspect Yun XX-hyeon or participate in the interrogation of the suspect, and ultimately was not retained as defense counsel for the above suspect. In addition, with respect to the above suspect, a detention warrant was issued and he was prosecuted while in custody. There is nothing in the record to suggest any circumstance that would lead a court to find legal interest to be lacking or extinguished if the Claimant filed a quasi-appeal against the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case. The Supreme Court has decided on the merits on the premise that legal interest exists even when a defense counsel’s participation was denied during the interrogation of a suspect and the interrogation procedure had ended (see Supreme Court Decision 2008MO793 dated 2008. 9. 12.); the same should apply where visitation is denied during the interrogation of a suspect.
Accordingly, even if the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case has already ended, the Claimant may challenge it by filing a quasi-appeal under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act; thus, the Claimant’s constitutional complaint regarding the denial of visitation in this case fails to satisfy the subsidiarity requirement and is unlawful.

C. 결론
The right of visitation and communication of a “person who intends to become defense counsel,” which the Claimant alleges was infringed by the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case, cannot be said to be a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution, and therefore the Claimant’s petition regarding the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case lacks the possibility of infringement of a fundamental right. Moreover, because the Claimant did not go through the quasi-appeal procedure under Article 417 of the Criminal Procedure Act, the subsidiarity requirement is also not satisfied.
Accordingly, the constitutional complaint concerning the Prosecutor’s denial of visitation in this case is unlawful in any event and must be dismissed."}

A. Alien detention system under the Immigration Control Act

(1) Detention under the Immigration Control Act means “enforcement activity by which an immigration control official takes and confines a person who has reasonable grounds to be suspected of falling under a person subject to deportation under Article 46(1) of the Immigration Control Act in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice, for the purpose of deporting such person” (Article 2 No. 11 of the Immigration Control Act). Detention under the Immigration Control Act includes “detention for the determination of a person subject to deportation” prescribed in Article 51 and “detention for the execution of a deportation order” prescribed in the 심판대상조항.

(2) According to the 심판대상조항, the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may detain an alien subject to a deportation order (hereinafter referred to as a “person subject to deportation”) in an alien detention room, alien detention center, or any other place designated by the Minister of Justice (hereinafter referred to as a “detention facility”) until such person can be repatriated when immediate repatriation outside the Republic of Korea is impossible for reasons such as the absence of a passport or lack of transportation. Detention under the 심판대상조항 is intended to secure the execution of a deportation order where a deportation order has been issued upon determining that an alien falls under a person subject to deportation, but immediate execution is impossible, and is distinguished from detention under Article 51 of the Immigration Control Act, which secures the physical presence of an alien in order to examine whether the alien falls under a person subject to deportation.

The 심판대상조항 states that detention is permissible “until such person can be repatriated,” and thus, in the wording of the statute, imposes no limitation on the detention period; instead, where the period of detention exceeds 3 months, prior approval from the Minister of Justice must be obtained every 3 months, and if such approval is not obtained, detention must be released (Article 63(2) and (3) of the Immigration Control Act). In addition, a person detained in a detention facility pursuant to the 심판대상조항 may file an objection with the Minister of Justice (Article 63(6) and Article 55 of the Immigration Control Act), and the head of a local immigration office or foreigners office may, ex officio or upon request of the detainee, temporarily release the detainee from detention by requiring the deposit of a security deposit not exceeding 20 million won and attaching restrictions on residence or other necessary conditions, after considering the detainee’s circumstances, reasons for request for release, assets, and other matters (Article 65(1) of the Immigration Control Act).

B. Issues and Standard of Review

(1) Detention under the 심판대상조항 is a compulsory measure by which a person subject to deportation is taken and confined in a detention facility in order to secure execution of a deportation order when immediate execution of the deportation order is impossible, and thus restricts the detainee’s freedom of the person (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29). Therefore, the issue in this case is whether the 심판대상조항 infringes freedom of the person by violating the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction, which is the limiting principle on restriction of fundamental rights, and the principle of due process under Article 12 of the Constitution.

(2) Immigration control administration is state administration that promotes the national interest and security by appropriately controlling and adjusting the entry and exit of nationals and foreigners and the stay of foreigners. Among matters relating to immigration control, matters concerning the entry and domestic stay of foreigners are necessary for performing the functions of a sovereign state and lie within the domain of broad policy discretion (see Constitutional Court 2005. 3. 31. 2003HEONMA87; Constitutional Court 2014. 4. 24. 2011HEONMA474 et al.). Detention under the 심판대상조항, which is carried out to secure execution of a deportation order, may be regarded as part of immigration control administration.

However, freedom of the person under Article 12(1) of the Constitution is the most fundamental minimum freedom necessary to realize human dignity and value, and serves as the premise for the guarantee of all fundamental rights (see Constitutional Court 2020. 9. 24. 2017HEONBA157 et al.). By its nature, it is a human right, and whether it is recognized does not vary depending on whether one has lawful status of stay in the country. Therefore, a strict standard of review must be applied to whether the 심판대상조항 infringes freedom of the person.

C. Constitutional Opinion of Justices Yoon Nam-seok, Lee Seok-tae, Kim Gi-yeong, Moon Hyeong-bae, and Lee Mi-seon

(1) Whether the principle of prohibition of excessive restriction is violated

(a) Legitimacy of purpose and appropriateness of means

The legislative purpose of the 심판대상조항 is to appropriately control and adjust the entry, exit, and stay of foreigners, thereby promoting national security and order, by taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea so that deportation orders may be executed easily and efficiently. Such legislative purpose is legitimate, and taking and confining persons subject to deportation in a detention facility until they can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea is an effective means of securing execution of a deportation order; thus, appropriateness of means is also recognized.

(b) Minimum infringement and balance of interests

However, the 심판대상조항 fails to satisfy the minimum infringement requirement and the balance of interests requirement for the following reasons.

1) Detention under the 심판대상조항 is a compulsory measure temporarily and provisionally taken to secure execution when a deportation order cannot be executed immediately upon issuance (see Constitutional Court 2018. 2. 22. 2017HEONGA29). Yet the 심판대상조항 merely provides that a person subject to deportation may be detained until such person can be repatriated outside the Republic of Korea, and does not set an upper limit on the detention period, thereby making indefinite detention possible.

Detention by which a person subject to deportation is temporarily and provisionally confined in a specific place for the purpose of executing a deportation order can, by its very nature, be deemed justified only when the person is confined within a reasonable period necessary for the execution of the deportation order.
